articles.title_orig: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including a doctor and a child, Health Ministry says
articles.title_zh: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including a doctor and a child, Health Ministry says
articles.content_orig:
Medical staff inspect damage to Nasser Hospital after it was hit by an Israeli airstrike overnight in Khan Younis, Gaza Strip on Thursday. Abdel Kareem Hana/AP hide caption
KHAN YOUNIS, Gaza Strip — An Israeli airstrike targeting the Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a general surgeon, and wounded at least 28 more, Gaza's Health Ministry said.
The strike was carried out early Thursday, according to the Israeli military, which said it struck a Hamas commander and other militants, without providing evidence.
The Gaza Health Ministry said the strike hit the hospital's surgical wing and that a doctor, Rizk Abu Shaira, was among the dead. Inside the building, parts of several floors were either severely damaged or destroyed. Debris was scattered across hospital beds and equipment, and rebar dangled from the ceiling where the munition had penetrated.
British surgeon Goher Rahbour, who is volunteering at Nasser Hospital, said that the strike occurred just after midnight and shook the whole building.
"It was extremely smoky," said Rahbour, who was on the fourth floor of the surgical department when the bomb hit. The recovery area on the same floor was reduced to rubble, he said.
He said he had been operating alongside Abu Shaira just hours before the strike. "Lovely guy, happy and smiling," he said.
Nasser Hospital in the city of Khan Younis is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza, whose healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by a yearslong war.
The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals across Gaza, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters. It has also destroyed medical equipment and supplies and killed or detained hundreds of healthcare workers.
In armed conflict, hospitals and their staff are protected under international humanitarian law. A hospital can lose its protected status, however, if it is used for military purposes.
In a statement on Thursday, the military said Hamas had "established a presence within the hospital complex" and that the commander had turned it "into a headquarters."
Israeli forces have previously attacked Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed five journalists — including AP contributor Mariam Dagga — when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex.
The war in Gaza started on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage. Since then, Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,600 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which is part of the Hamas-run government but whose figures are generally considered reliable by the international community.
Israel has continued to strike Gaza despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire and controls at least 60% of the enclave. Since the truce went into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes and gunfire have killed 1,622 people, health authorities say. Five Israeli soldiers have also been killed during that period.

articles.title_orig: Boy found alive after 6 days lost in Australian wilderness: "He's grounded for life"
articles.title_zh: Boy found alive after 6 days lost in Australian wilderness: "He's grounded for life"
articles.content_orig:
A 17-year-old boy with autism was found alive Thursday after six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands.
The boy, whom police identified only as William, had begun camping with a teenage friend when he disappeared last Friday near Walhalla, a former gold-mining town 185 kilometers (115 miles) east of Melbourne, police said.
A police helicopter crew found him surrounded by wilderness lying asleep on a flat rock beside a creek, and he was later reunited with his mother. William was in good spirits and mostly in good health, the police statement said.
Video shot from the rescue helicopter showed he was shirtless and sunburned. He was wearing shorts and boots and was using towels as blankets.
"I'm just over the moon that he's alive," his mother, Elizabeth, told reporters. The AP has decided not to provide her family name to avoid identifying her son.
"And he's never leaving the house again. He's grounded for life. He's not going anywhere ever again," she joked.
Police video showed Elizabeth embrace her son after the rescue helicopter landed to complete its mission.
William was later taken to a hospital for his health to be monitored, police said.
"Amazingly, William is in good spirits and for the most part, in good health," they said in the statement.
William's family have said he has Level 2 autism. That requires "substantial support," according to the Australian advocacy group Autism360.
Such a person may have marked deficits in verbal and non-verbal social communication and rely heavily on routines and predictable activities. Disruption can cause significant distress.
The Southern Hemisphere spring weather had been mild for the past week in the alpine region where William was lost and there had been little rain.
Elizabeth had dropped off her son and his friend last Friday for a weekend of camping. William walked a short distance from the campsite to the drop-off location to collect more camping equipment but never returned to his friend, police said.
After becoming lost, William trekked for days up and down "some very steep terrain," Acting Police Inspector Jason Benbow said.
He spent the last two days where he was found at the creek, trapped by the steepness of his surrounds 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the his camp site, Benbow said.
"He woke up to the sound of the helicopter, gave them a thumbs up and they winched him to safety," Benbow told reporters.
The extensive police search for him involved more than 100 emergency services personnel and volunteers.
There have been other dramatic rescues in Australia's wilderness in recent years.
In 2025, a German tourist was found alive in Australia's remote Outback, 12 days after she went missing. She was found just a day after officials and local media said an Australian surfer , who had been feared lost at sea, was rescued after spending a night on an uninhabited island miles from where they had walked into the water.
In 2019, an Australian woman missing for three days was rescued after the SOS message she scrawled in the sand was spotted on a surveillance camera.
The successful rescues have included animals as well. Last year, a runaway dog was captured after a 529-day adventure in Australia as she roamed an island teeming with kangaroos, possums, koala bears and penguins.
Agence  France-Presse contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Mammoth crowds greet Pope Leo on return to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.title_zh: Mammoth crowds greet Pope Leo on return to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.content_orig:
Lee el artículo en español
Riding on horseback to visit the most isolated Andean areas of his community, distributing food amid the Covid-19 pandemic, or wearing rubber boots in the water and mud of floods: this is how many Peruvians remember the man who is now Pope Leo XIV.
Robert Prevost was in the trenches and alongside his people during Peru’s most difficult moments, and many of these memories were likely front of mind among the millions who gathered to welcome the pope on his visit to his adopted homeland on Wednesday.
Pope Leo arrived in Callao city, near Lima, to a hero’s welcome with spectators at the airport waving flags and cheering as he stepped out of his plane and waved to the crowd. He was received by high-ranking officials including President Keiko Fujimori and Foreign Minister Carlos Espá.
Later, a sea of supporters lined the streets to salute him as his motorcade drove him to the government palace in the capital. The Vatican says an estimated 3 million people turned out, the largest crowd of his papacy so far. Earlier this week, roughly 2.5 million attended a mass he held in Argentina.
In a speech in front of Fujimori and the country’s political leaders, Leo said his return to Peru holds a “very special meaning” for him.
“That is why I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am also returning to my homeland,” he said.
Referencing the time he spent in the country, Leo said he had been made to “feel like one of their own” with people welcoming him into their homes and sharing with him “some good ceviche,” a traditional Peruvian fish dish. He also credited the country with “forming me as a shepherd.”
The pope’s trip to Peru, which will include visits to Cusco and Chiclayo, is widely seen as a homecoming for a pontiff who knows the country in depth and is a Peruvian citizen. In fact, he will receive a new Peruvian ID card that will list Chiclayo as his address.
A young Prevost first arrived in the South American country as a missionary in 1985. The years that followed shaped his leadership style, which would later lead him to become the successor to the late Pope Francis.
“I think he was heroic in many ways; he risked becoming ill. We lost 11 priests and a bishop emeritus during that time,” Father José Del Rosario recalls of the most difficult days of the pandemic.
Padre Robert, as he is known in Spanish in Peru, traveled more than 700 kilometers (435 miles) from Chiclayo to the Diocese of Callao, a province bordering the capital, Lima, where he served as apostolic administrator.
“He came every two weeks in his little car; he came alone in a simple pickup truck,” explained Del Rosario, parish priest and rector of the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Mount Carmel of La Legua, who worked closely with the then-bishop.
Pope! Amigo! Peruvians remember the young American priest who became pope
Prevost distributed food and everything needed by a population that lived under lockdown for months, while also offering spiritual guidance during the crisis.
“He gave us a lot of hope and cared for our people, a man who was very close to the people … and also very humble,” Del Rosario added.
Peru recorded more than 219,000 deaths , according to Johns Hopkins University figures, and one of the highest coronavirus mortality rates in the world. In Lima, and especially in the regions, terrifying scenes unfolded outside hospitals, with sick people collapsing in the street due to the shortage of oxygen, one of the key tools for treating the virus.
In Chiclayo, Bishop Prevost launched a fundraising campaign to purchase an oxygen plant. Together with Caritas Chiclayo, the bishop appealed to authorities and sectors of civil society and managed to raise more than US$380,000 for not just one but two oxygen plants.
Janinna Sesa, former director of Caritas Chiclayo, worked with the bishop for eight years, including during the pandemic, the flooding caused by the coastal El Niño in 2017, and Cyclone Yaku in 2023.
“We were always on the front lines, especially during disasters like the coastal El Niño phenomenon. He was the person who put on his boots and waded into the water; he helped people. He was very approachable and very kind,” Sesa told CNN.
Before leaving for Rome in 2023, after the late Pope Francis appointed him prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, Bishop Prevost also led appeals for aid for the more than 10,000 people affected by flooding caused by Cyclone Yaku in the north of the country.
“I ask you to be generous; I ask you to open your hearts so that we can help one another and move forward, as we have done in other times of crisis,” Prevost said in a video while standing in the water in the district of Illimo, in the Lambayeque region.
Examine the power held by popes throughout history
The assistance and response led by Prevost in the face of the massive arrival of Venezuelan migrants in 2018 was comprehensive and had a different vision from that of the country’s other regions.
Peru received more than 1.6 million Venezuelans through November 2025, the second-highest number in the region after Colombia. More than 20,000 of them passed through Chiclayo, and more than 3,500 families settled in the region, according to figures from the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking of the Diocese of Chiclayo. Prevost also promoted this commission to assist migrants and combat human trafficking.
First American pope marks July 4 on migrant island with plea for ‘compassion and generosity’
“The migration flow descended upon us, with thousands of migrants out on the streets, sleeping there, and the parishes serving as shelters,” Sesa recalled.
Father Robert was concerned not only with providing food and collecting clothing, blankets, and medicine, but also with building the San Vicente de Paúl village, which took them in at Puerto Etén.
“His simplicity, the peace he conveys, that serenity Monsignor Prevost had when listening to people — I still see it in Pope Leo XIV…. He welcomed us with such warmth, with so much love,” Lisbeth Díaz, a Venezuelan resident of Chiclayo and member of the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking, told CNN.
Prevost prioritized regularizing their legal status so they could work and integrate into society.
Prevost created spaces for dialogue and encouraged many people to raise their voices to denounce abuses during the internal conflict the country experienced beginning in the 1980s and to openly discuss the social reality during the authoritarian regime of the late President Alberto Fujimori in the 1990s.
At the Augustinian mission in Trujillo, the current pontiff and his seminarians traveled through towns and parishes in Andean areas, staging dramatizations that reflected the violence faced by peasants to encourage conversations that would help heal the trauma and pain they had suffered.
Prevost also participated in collecting signatures for the creation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), which investigated the violence between 1980 and 2000 and human rights abuses, particularly in rural Peru. Trujillo and the parishes led by the current pontiff collected the largest number of signatures.
Leo XIV is a pope forged in Peru. The nearly two decades he spent in the land he adopted as his own profoundly shaped his ministry and set him on the path to the papacy. As a bishop, Prevost was a pastor close to his flock, and at the Vatican, one of his closest collaborators is the Reverend Edgard Rimaycuna, a native of Chiclayo.
His work in South America and his leadership of the Order of Saint Augustine caught the attention of Pope Francis, who first appointed him bishop of Chiclayo and later brought him to Rome, where he went on to hold one of the most important positions in the Vatican and also became a cardinal. This made him a candidate in the 2025 conclave.

articles.title_orig: Google Agrees to Privacy in Spirit Airlines Data Sale
articles.title_zh: Google Agrees to Privacy in Spirit Airlines Data Sale
articles.content_orig:
If you care about privacy, don’t feed your own personal information into a chatbot , which—among other concerns—could use it to train AI tools. Employees, though, mostly don’t have a choice.
A new, multibillion-dollar industry is dedicated to selling and buying work files and emails to companies seeking fresh sources of data to improve their AI models, and it’s only getting bigger . Data privacy laws tend to focus on consumer protections and rarely consider the rights of workers who create that information. What happens when your doctor’s notes, employee contracts, and Slack gossip are fed into the machine?
An agreement reached this week between Google and a union representing an unlikely workforce—flight attendants—could reveal a more permanent answer by creating a process that might reliably separate the data that workers produce from their own personal information. A judge still needs to approve the agreement next week.
The first-of-its-kind deal is part of the liquidation process for Spirit Airlines, which suddenly ceased operations earlier this year . In August, representatives for the budget airline said in a legal brief that it would be selling decades’ worth of data to Google for $10 million ; Google said it would not receive personal information as part of the sale. But the union, the 55,000-member Association for Flight Attendants, argued that Google’s proposed safeguards would not prevent serious privacy violations for Spirit Airlines flight attendants, whose records—including 1.99 billion emails, 664 million Microsoft Teams messages, and employee travel and training information, all dating back to 1986—would be included in the sale.
The revised deal requires Spirit to hire a third-party data de-identification company, called Tonic AI, to exclude information that could potentially be associated with individual consumers or employees. Tonic will also be charged with ensuring that data, once de-identified, cannot be relinked to specific people. Google has promised to maintain the data in this new, de-identified form.
Many sensitive records will be excluded from the sale, including employee medical records, documents related to employee investigations and labor relations, and information about industry-wide safety management systems. In early November, a trade organization representing airlines chimed in on the sale, arguing that including that information could make employees less willing to come forward to report safety issues through voluntary programs , which are widely regarded as critical to the US aviation industry’s strong safety record.
The proposed agreement also includes an opt-out clause. Google can choose to renege on the sale if the data-cleaning process reduces the assets by more than 8 percent. Google didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Association for Flight Attendants president Sara Nelson tells WIRED she’s as surprised as anyone that flight attendants are at the forefront of AI-related workers’ rights issues, which often focus on employees who, willingly or unwillingly, train their machine replacements.
“It’s very hard to replace a flight attendant—you’d need a high-functioning robot, and that seems to be further off,” she says. “What this shows is that this is an issue even in jobs you think are most protected from AI. This is an issue for everyone.”
She said the union will immediately begin to demand that other airlines include worker-data-protection clauses in their labor agreements. “If you’re not willing to meet these standards for your workers, we’re going to shame you,” she says. The Association for Flight Attendants has begun meeting with state-level politicians to craft legislation that would write worker data protections into law.
Ari Ezra Waldman, a professor at the UC Irvine School of Law who studies law and technology, calls the proposed settlement “a pretty good outcome” for Spirit Airlines employees. “From now on, unions will know to negotiate to protect the privacy rights in the event of future sales of data assets,” he wrote to WIRED in an email. He points to another, and maybe easier, alternative: Banning the sale of data altogether. “Privacy protections are necessary now more than ever,” he says.
Tech leaders have argued that workers understand that their information will train AI models, which will ultimately make their lives better and easier. “You have to think of the upside, the abundance that AI can result in,” one executive told WIRED this month .
Nelson says US workers aren’t buying the upside of AI and that they’re part of the wider electorate that seems to be growing warier of the tech by the day . She says the vision of AI abundance is “a fantasyland of people in boardrooms with beanbags who wear hoodies.”

articles.title_orig: COP31: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'
articles.title_zh: COP31: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone".
Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.
But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.
In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.
Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.
He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office .
Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.
As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri.
Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates."
As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.
This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year.
The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.
Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words.
"The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said.
On tackling the causes of climate change, Burnham said his government remained committed to meeting the country's target of net zero by 2050 whilst also getting bills down.
He said key to this was cutting our "dependence on fossil fuels" and increasing electrification - the amount of our energy needs met from renewable electricity.
The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.
Turkey, the co-hosts of COP31, wants a key outcomes of this year's summit to be a commitment by countries to meet 35% of their energy supply from electricity by 2035. Currently, it is around a fifth.
But Burnham has been accused of having double standards.
"The Prime Minister simply cannot call for clean power across the world while saying yes to more fossil fuels in the UK," said Beth John, climate adviser at Oxfam.
Last month, the government approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea on the grounds that it provided energy security.
And in the budget last month Chancellor John Healey announced a funding cut to the Warm Homes Plan, which provides grants and loans to support the installation of heat pumps.
Whilst this week there has been media speculation that the government is considering watering down electric car sales targets, although the government insists no decision has been made.
Successfully switching petrol and diesel cars to EVs and moving from gas boilers to electric-powered heat pumps are key ways to achieve the 35% electrification target .
Although there was no royal presence this year, King Charles III sent a message ahead of Burnham's speech.
"As the world gathers for Cop31, I can only hope that this same spirit of partnership and common purpose can help inspire the collective action that our planet – and future generations – so urgently need.
"Our children and grandchildren will not judge us by the promises we made, but by what we chose to do."
Burnham was the only G7 leader to speak at this year's conference in a sign of faltering support for the COP process - something he acknowledged in his speech.
In an almost word for word copy of Sir Keir Starmer's address last year he said: "The consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate has gone, and the reality is now the world will reach 1.5 degrees."
Other leaders expected to speak on Thursday include many island states like Tonga, Tuvalu and the Solomon Islands.
For these nations, the impact of climate change is already at their front door. With most of their land just metres above sea level, rising water levels have caused many to abandon their homes in recent years.
Last year, Australia - the co-host of the COP31 summit - opened up the world's first climate visa for Tuvalu citizens wanting to evacuate.
The first intake was massively oversubscribed, with more than a third of the population entering the ballot.
As glaciers continue to melt and oceans expand, average sea levels are expected to keep climbing and potentially accelerate. The World Meteorological Organisation said on the opening day of this conference the global mean sea level was at its highest level since records began.

articles.title_orig: China’s diaspora crackdown reaches deep into Europe, report finds
articles.title_zh: China’s diaspora crackdown reaches deep into Europe, report finds
articles.content_orig:
THE HAGUE — Beijing is overseeing nearly 1,250 overseas policing outposts in more than 90 countries to crack down on dissidents, according to a report by a human rights advocacy organization.
The report described Europe as a hotspot with hundreds of Beijing’s policing offices across some two dozen European countries, which it said exposed China’s growing attempts to control its diaspora.
Researchers at the Spain-based organization, Safeguard Defenders, gathered open-source evidence from the Chinese Party-state to examine the extent to which the Chinese diaspora is monitored, surveilled and policed around the world.
These policing outposts “act as the Chinese Communist Party operatives for community surveillance and enforcement abroad,” according to the report.
The report lands at an awkward time for Europe’s trade officials. Ditte Juul Jørgensen, head of the EU’s trade department — which has been working to balance the trade relationship with Beijing — will meet with China’s Vice Minister of Commerce Ling Ji in Brussels on Thursday.
Europe is attempting to walk a fine line with its relations with Beijing. EU legislation proposed in January seeks to kick risky Chinese suppliers out of Europe’s most critical industries over cybersecurity concerns, while supply chain dependencies and political coercion remain ongoing challenges. The EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas has also raised concerns about what she said was China’s enabling of Russia’s war in Ukraine and credible reports of China training Russia’s military .
The report builds on initial revelations from Safeguard Defenders in 2022 that identified more than 100 facilities around the world, which the NGO described as overseas outposts of China’s security apparatus. Back then, that report said Beijing announced its “first batch” of “30 overseas police service stations in 25 cities in 21 countries.”
Following the revelations, some governments denounced the overseas police stations as illegal, and some pursued criminal investigations, the NGO said in its latest report. In response, Beijing claimed the stations had been closed, it added.
“Far from closing, the evidence shows expansion: today more than 10 police forces from five Chinese provinces work through a global network of Chinese Communist Party operatives abroad,” the new report says.
The latest paper was presented at a conference hosted by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC), a gathering of 52 cross-party lawmakers from 30 countries that campaigns for a more coordinated response to the Chinese Communist Party. Policymakers raised numerous concerns at the event in The Hague earlier this month — about what they considered security threats of critical infrastructure, trade dependencies and potential risks from a future conflict between China and Taiwan that would disrupt shipping.
The Chinese foreign ministry and state media have previously called IPAC an “anti-China” group and accused it of spreading disinformation and interfering in China’s internal affairs, particularly over Taiwan.
China’s Ministry for Foreign Affairs and its European Union mission didn’t respond to requests for comment on the report. China has previously denied running overseas police stations and says it doesn’t interfere in other countries’ internal affairs and that it respects international law.
In 2023, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson rejected the term “police stations,” saying the “institutions helped overseas Chinese who could not return to China due to the pandemic, renew their driving licence and perform physical examination.”
These 1,250 offices were “the tip of the iceberg,” according to the NGO, which said it was conservative in how it mapped and linked them to China’s policing system. To be counted, they had to be officially connected to China’s police or prosecutors and have open-source evidence of overseas activities, report author Laura Harth said. This meant broader influence or interference operations were excluded.
“All of them serve to control and instill fear in diaspora communities … all of them represent a standing national security risk,” she said.
Slovakian MEP Miriam Lexmann, who is part of the European Parliament’s trade committee and China delegation — lawmakers tasked with maintaining and managing legislative ties between the EU and China — said people needed to become more aware of the security threats posed by China.
“It means that our free countries are no longer free anymore for everyone because they are not able to guarantee freedom of speech, freedom of behavior to people who are in our country,” she told POLITICO in reference to the operations.
China’s surveillance through facial recognition and interference in communications was “the exact behavior of the former Soviet Stasi,” she said, but worse since the technology is now much more sophisticated.
The main concern expressed by lawmakers attending the IPAC conference was China’s relationship with Russia, and its help in propping up the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine. Their discussions included what this could mean for a future conflict and war on two fronts if Beijing were to try and take Taiwan militarily while NATO countries were attacked by Russia.
“The road to escalation in the Taiwan Strait can run right through what’s happening in Ukraine and in Kyiv,” said Dutch lawmaker Jan Paternotte, who co-chaired the IPAC conference.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft confirms Windows security updates installation issues
articles.title_zh: Microsoft confirms Windows security updates installation issues
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft has confirmed reports that the November 2026 security updates are failing to install on Windows 11 systems with the October preview update.
This follows widespread reports that the KB5132061 update fails to install , with affected users seeing the installation process lock midway and then trigger 0x800f0989 or 0x800f0993 errors.
"When attempting to install the November 2026 Windows security update (the Originating KBs listed above), some devices might be unable to complete the installation. Affected devices might repeatedly attempt to install the update or display error code 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993," Microsoft said in a service update seen by BleepingComputer.
"This issue affects a limited number of devices that installed the October 2026 non-security preview update (KB5127936). Devices that did not install the October 2026 non-security preview update are not affected."
Microsoft also told IT administrators that the installation issues will resolve automatically for all affected customers by Friday morning and that end users do not need to take any action to receive the fix.
"All affected devices should be repaired in 24 to 48 hours starting from November 11, 2026, 10am PT. Once your device receives the repair, it will automatically download and install the November 2026 security update via Windows Update," it added.
The company also urged admins still receiving reports of installation issues after 48 hours to contact Microsoft Support.
This is not the first time Microsoft has had to address Windows update installation issues since the start of the year. In March, it had to pull a buggy Windows 11 non-security preview update (KB5079391) because of 0x80073712 errors during installation.
In May, it also fixed installation failures and 0x800f0922 errors when deploying the May 2026 Windows 11 security update ( KB5089549 ).
More recently, in June, Microsoft warned users that they may encounter issues installing the latest monthly updates and see 0x80073712 or 0x800f0993 errors on some Windows devices upgraded to Windows 11 24H2 or 25H2.

Nvidia LIVE updates: Nvidia's board has been working with an outside firm as it mulls removing Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer, claims a WSJ report. This meeting comes after Jensen Huang's admission of having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, a row has erupted, with the United States launching a 'national security' probe into the matter. ...Read More
US officials have stated that they have reason to believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese intelligence asset. Jensen Huang has not named Huang Le while admitting to his affair.
Concerns were also raised after it was found that Alice Huang was a managing director at Megaspeed, which is a Singapore-based firm and Nvidia's main cloud partner for the Asia-Pacific region.
US officials have alleged that through Jensen Huang, Alice Huang may have helped China secure Nvidia's AI chips, which Beijing has been prohibited from acquiring.
Amid this row, a New York Times report has claimed that Jensen Huang had a second affair with Nvidia vice president Kimberly Powell, who directly reports to him.
Jensen Huang LIVE Updates: Shares of Nvidia, the chipmaker at the center of the global artificial intelligence boom, tumbled early Thursday with the tenure of CEO Jensen Huang threatened by revelations of an affair with a woman reported to be a suspected Chinese spy.
The company's stock has been under pressure for weeks, both because of reporting about the affair and questions about a potential bubble in the AI sector.
Shares slid 7% to $161.37 before the opening bell, 34% below the company's all-time high reached just over a month ago.
The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a second affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, and analysts said that may force the board to oust him.
“What seemed impossible a week ago is now a reality as we cannot see Jensen running Nvidia as CEO at this point and the stock/company should be valued without him as CEO," wrote Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.
Nvidia is now valued at more than $4 trillion and has been a major driver in the technology sector. It is one of the reasons the tech heavy Nasdaq Composite index raced higher for most of this year and also part of the reason the index has slumped 7% in the past month.
As the crisis unfolds at Nvidia, shares of rivals like AMD, Advanced Micro Devices, and Broadcom have moved sharply higher.
CoreWeave, however slid nearly 9%. Nvidia owns a stake of approximately 13% in the a data center and cloud company. (AP)
Jensen Huang LIVE Updates: Long-dated US Treasury yields declined when trading resumed on Thursday, as turmoil surrounding Nvidia weighed on technology stocks and prompted investors to seek safer assets.
The movements in yields were modest but held steady despite a recovery in oil prices, indicating some demand for safe-haven assets. Yields on 30-year US Treasuries fell by as much as three basis points to 5.32%, while 10-year yields remained largely unchanged at around 4.99%. Cash trading was closed on Wednesday due to the Veterans Day holiday.
Nvidia is a key indicator of the technology investment boom, which has supported expectations of US economic growth and pushed bond yields higher. Its chips play a crucial role in the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure, making any prospect of a replacement for Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang a source of concern for investors, given his central role in the company.
Jensen Huang LIVE Updates: Technology shares came under pressure Thursday as investors kept a nervous eye on AI giant Nvidia, whose influential boss Jensen Huang is facing a board revolt amid a probe into an affair with a woman accused of spying for China.
Reports of another affair, between Huang and a senior Nvidia executive, piled on the pressure and reportedly prompted an emergency board meeting late Wednesday.
Shares in Nvidia, which is due to report quarterly earnings next Tuesday, slid about six percent in pre-market trading.
"A leadership scandal at one of the world's biggest companies is enough to bring the tech stock rally to a halt, and the Nasdaq is pointing to a lower open," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at trading group XTB.
She added that the Nvidia fallout was "helping to spur a rotation into European markets that are traditionally low-tech".
London, Paris and Frankfurt all climbed in midday deals. (AFP)
Jensen Huang LIVE Updates: Megaspeed, the data center company at the center of the scandal engulfing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, pledged Thursday to cooperate with an investigation into potential risks to U.S. national security.
Nvidia’s board, meanwhile, was reportedly meeting to discuss Huang’s future after revelations that he was having an affair with a former Megaspeed executive suspected of being a Chinese government agent.
There was no word as of early Thursday on any outcome from those discussions.
In its first statement since Huang admitted to having an affair with a Chinese woman and former executive of the company, Singapore-headquartered Megaspeed International said Thursday that it takes its obligation to comply with U.S. export control laws “extremely seriously.”
“Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the U.S. government,” said the statement signed by its chairman and CEO, Tan Yong Pong, who also goes by James Tan.
Nvidia has said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.
Details about Huang’s affair with the woman are unclear. The New York Times reported she was Alice Huang, who also goes by the name Huang Le, and was a top executive at Megaspeed. The company prominently touts a partnership with Nvidia on its website. (AP)
Jensen Huang LIVE Updates: Fresh turbulence hit global stocks on Thursday as a spy scandal threatened to oust chip giant Nvidia’s CEO, while US Treasury yields touched 5% again and the dollar reached a 19-month high on firming US rate rise bets.
There was early cheer for Europe where the comparatively tech-light STOXX 600 hit its first record high since August, but elsewhere the strains were showing. [.EU]
Asian markets suffered falls overnight after reports that Nvidia's board had met to decide the fate of long-time leader Jensen Huang sent the company's shares diving nearly 7% in premarket US trading. [.N]
Chinese tech firms that use Nvidia chips for their AI models fell heavily in Hong Kong. Alibaba and Tencent tumbled 6.7% and 2.6% respectively amid concerns that Washington may now curb access to offshore datacentres with the most advanced processors.
Many of the other global market issues were back in play too. (Reuters)

Megaspeed International announced the probe after Jensen Huang, Nvidia's CEO, admitted to having an affair, reportedly with a former Megaspeed executive who the United States suspects of being a Chinese intelligence asset.

articles.title_orig: US envoys arrive in Moscow for Ukraine talks with Vladimir Putin
articles.title_zh: US envoys arrive in Moscow for Ukraine talks with Vladimir Putin
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said his country's military was again facing "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade service, meaning Kyiv was struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
Starshield is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company and plays a vital role in military operations.
Ukraine was "trying to clear up all circumstances with the American side", Zelensky said.
His comments come as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
Kushner and Witkoff are then expected to travel to Dublin, where they will meet Zelensky.
A similar issue with Starshield connectivity affected the front line in late October and lasted about a week before it was fixed. It remained unclear who ordered the temporary restrictions on Starshield services, with US officials and SpaceX offering differing explanations.
Zelensky said the current disruption had been ongoing for several days and was "helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine".
Videos shared by Russian media on Thursday showed Kushner and Witkoff disembarking a plane and being welcomed by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev with handshakes and hugs.
On Tuesday, Kushner said the US had seen "some openings and some opportunities" and that they would try to "make some progress" at the meeting with Putin.
The in-person talks with the Russian and Ukrainian presidents were only announced on Wednesday after two days of talks which were framed as centred around the postwar security architecture of Europe.
Nearly five years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow shows no sign of backing down from its maximalist demands for sovereign Ukrainian territory and for Western countries to give up any future commitment to protecting Kyiv in case of further attacks.
During the first years of the war, Europeans cut communications with the Kremlin and refused to engage with Russia directly.
However, in recent times many have grown concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin, and have been pushing for a seat at the negotiating table.
The talks in Abu Dhabi were led by the Americans and only included Russia and Ukraine, but Kushner said he and Witkoff would ask Putin to "give his blessing" to invite European representatives in future discussions - particularly with regards to the future configuration of their continent's security architecture.
Kushner also urged Europe to "identify one person to speak on their behalf" in the negotiations.
But the Russians have been opposed to the idea, citing Europe's support for Kyiv as an obstacle.
Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi, said he thought all parties had "moved closer to achieving peace" but that now "a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the United States, and on whether Europe comes to its senses".

Nvidia’s board meets over CEO’s future as the AI giant reels from the China spy scandal. Five people are dead after a building collapse in Brooklyn. And, how American Legion halls are adapting as the veteran population shrinks.
Here’s what to know today.
Nvidia’s board was addressing CEO Jensen Huang’s future at the company last night, two sources familiar with the matter told NBC News, as the American chipmaking giant reeled from the scandal surrounding its leader’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy .
This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox.
Nvidia shares dropped almost 9% in after-hours trading amid multiple reports that Huang’s future hung in the balance. The company’s board met following a new report in The New York Times that he also had a relationship with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.
Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the newspaper reported that Huang had an affair with another woman, in addition to a woman who was suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Huang wrote in a note to employees Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to his wife,” though he did not specify details. NBC News reported that U.S. intelligence agencies had determined that the first woman, Alice Huang , was a Chinese intelligence operative.
China has dismissed the allegations, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
“The U.S. side should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives as a pretext for implementing technological blockades,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters today.
At least five people died and more than a dozen others were hurt when an apartment building collapsed in New York City, officials said, sparking a search by firefighters through piles of rubble. Seven children and a firefighter were among the people injured, the Fire Department of New York said.
A man told NBC New York that his brother, Jose Luis Caguana, was killed in the collapse. Caguana, a 26-year-old immigrant from Ecuador, was working in construction to support his family, including his pregnant wife.
The collapse occurred at a four-unit building dating from 1930 in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn on the edge of a construction site where a one-story building had been previously demolished. It was unclear what caused the collapse.

Colom’s victory will give Democrats at least 55 Senate seats, as he’s the eighth Democrat to flip a Republican-held seat for the year. Republicans will have 44 seats. The only Senate race left to be called is in Alaska. Read more about Colom’s historic win.
Colom’s win — and the results and exit polls from the midterm elections nationwide — tell a clear story: A country that elected Trump in 2024 to lower the cost of living deemed him a failure. “There’s so much. … It’s not just the president,” said Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert, whose red district in Colorado became an unexpectedly close race that’s yet to be called. “We collectively failed.” How other GOP lawmakers have tiptoed around Trump.

articles.title_zh: Ireland under pressure to stop sending Russia an ingredient vital to its war on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:

After being moored along Ireland’s boggy River Shannon estuary this week, the 120-metre-long (400-foot-long) cargo ship Karin set sail for Russia.
The vessel was laden with a bulk cargo of white powder that can be forged into weapons which are vital to Moscow’s war on Ukraine .
Alumina, a key ingredient in aluminium, goes into products from toothpaste and lipstick to missiles and drones.
A Russian-owned plant in southern Ireland operates as Europe’s biggest alumina refinery, regularly sending shiploads of the substance directly to St Petersburg and other Russian ports.
Almost five years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, alumina has escaped European sanctions intended to hobble Russia’s economy . That leaves the refinery in Aughinish free to send its product to Russia, where experts say some ends up in weapons.
“The material is clearly ending up in military supplies," said Irish politician Ivana Bacik, who leads the opposition Labour Party.
“It would be unthinkable for Ireland to be contributing, even in that indirect way, to Putin’s war machine.”
Ireland faces mounting calls to halt the shipments as dozens of European leaders gather in Dublin this week to discuss support for Ukraine. A summit of the 47-nation European Political Community on Thursday is being followed by a meeting of European Union leaders.
Irish government minister Niall Collins said that "there’s absolutely no evidence" the material is ending up in military supply chains, though the government has declined to publish the findings of its investigation into the alumina shipments.
Aughinish Alumina said in a statement its product “has no connection to the Russian military supply chain” and that it hired an independent company to provide monthly audits to Irish authorities for “enhanced traceability.”
Alumina is a chemical compound refined from bauxite, a red ore mined primarily in Guinea, Australia and China. The chalky white substance can be smelted into aluminum, which is then forged with other, rarer elements to make strong, heat-resistant and flexible alloys used in missiles and aircraft; aluminum is also used in the manufacture of rocket fuel and explosives.
The Aughinish plant in County Limerick was built in the 1970s and bought in 2007 by Rusal, a Russian aluminum producer. The company was founded, and is still part-owned, by Oleg Deripaska, a sanctioned oligarch with ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin. Rusal makes virtually all of Russia's aluminum, according to the US and Australian governments.
While many cargo ships leave Aughinish bound for Europe and beyond, a steady stream of them heads straight to the port of St. Petersburg, according to data from MarineTraffic.
The activist group Alumina 22, which is lobbying to sanction the trade in alumina to Russia, estimated that between March and October some 491,307 metric tons of alumina from Ireland was shipped to Russia.
These shipments have grown in importance. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, two alumina factories – one in Australia, the other in Ukraine – stopped exporting to Russia, crimping its supplies by about 40 per cent, according to a 2026 report by the Economic Security Council of Ukraine, or ESCU.
Roughly 17 per cent of Rusal's alumina supply now comes from Ireland, according to ESCU.
An investigation by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and the Irish Times , published earlier this year, found that alumina from Aughinish is smelted in Russia into aluminum, with some of it sold to a metals trading company that supplies Russian defense contractors.
“Virtually everything that comes from Rusal is with a high probability ending up in the hands of Russian military enterprises,” said Olena Yurchenko, director of analytics, research and investigations at the ESCU.
Standing next to Irish President Micheál Martin in Dublin in June, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said: “Unfortunately, there are companies in Europe that are owned or effectively controlled by Russia and its sanctioned oligarchs. They keep supplying the aggressor with essential materials, even now.”
Mr Martin acknowledged that “we do not want to be in a position where material emanating from a plant in Ireland goes to support the Russian war machine.”
Ireland has not found evidence that is happening — but also no proof it is not, said Enterprise Minister Peter Burke, who is in charge of the country's sanctions enforcement. He said in July it had been impossible to prove Rusal’s assertion that alumina from Ireland is only used to make aluminum for export from Russia.
The Irish government has not published its findings, but it handed them to the European Commission, which drafts EU sanctions packages.
EU sanctions envoy David O’Sullivan said there is little doubt that “the alumina goes to smelters in Russia who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex”.
“I’ve read the government report. Personally, I think there’s no doubt the investigative journalists got it right,” he said in October in Dublin at a meeting organized by the Institute of International and European Affairs.
The European Parliament in July passed a non-binding motion calling for a ban on alumina exports to Russia. But alumina was not included in the EU’s 21st sanctions package against Russia that month. The EU’s executive European Commission, which draws up sanctions packages, is now sounding out member nations about the Irish alumina exports. Sanctions must be agreed upon unanimously by the bloc's 27 countries.
A commission spokesperson said in July that the bloc’s sanctions policy was “a delicate balance” between thwarting Russia’s war effort and limiting “negative impacts” on EU member nations, “especially considering that alumina is a critical raw material”.
Supporters of the plant point to the hundreds of jobs it provides, and to its role as a key source of alumina for European countries. Keeping supply lines open is especially important because of the chokehold on cargo traffic through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Mr Collins, who represents County Limerick in Ireland's parliament, said Ireland has been "hugely resolute in our support for the Ukrainians, and Ukraine hasn’t provided any evidence that Aughinish is doing anything adverse”.
Opposition politicians remain skeptical. Ms Bacik's left-of-center Labour Party supports a temporary nationalisation of the refinery, similar to when Ireland seized banks in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis. She says the refinery can ban exports to Russia and find other eager customers in Europe.
“We need to see much stronger action being taken on this from other EU countries if the Irish government isn’t willing to do the right thing here,” she said.
In Foynes, the wind-swept port town beside the plant, many work at Aughinish or know someone who does. But some locals have mixed feelings.
“It's too big a business for them to close it down,” said retired docker Joe Hanlon. “Too much employment for the government to get involved.”
But he said “of course they should”, if Ireland wants “to stop the war on Ukraine”.

articles.content_orig:
Morning Rundown: At least 8 dead in NYC building collapse, Jensen Huang’s fate in the balance, and Ukraine faces new Starshield disruptions
A Romanov sapphire weighing nearly 198 carats on a diamond-covered bracelet sold for more than 4.1 million Swiss francs ($4.9 million) at auction, vastly higher than the expected price range, Sotheby’s said.
The cushion-shaped sapphire attributed to onetime ownership of Russia’s imperial family was billed as a very rare stone, and had been expected to fetch between 850,000 and 1.7 million francs ($1 million and $2 million) at the Geneva auction late Wednesday.
The buyer, a private collector, wasn’t identified.
The 197.80-carat Ceylon sapphire likely came from the Mughal Empire in south Asia, made its way into Russia’s imperial jewels in the 19th century and is one of the most important surviving gemstones from the Russian court.
Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna, Czar Nicholas II’s mother, wore the sapphire at the Winter Palace Ball of 1903 — “widely regarded as the last great spectacle of Imperial Russia and immortalized in some of the most iconic images of the Romanov court,” the auction house said.
After the Russian Revolution, the sapphire was recorded in inventory before entering the Soviet government’s dispersal sales of imperial treasures, Sotheby’s said.

articles.title_zh: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years, before hundreds of thousands join protest
articles.content_orig:
Authorities in Spain say that despite pouring rain, some 120,000 citizens took to the streets of the capital, Madrid, on Wednesday evening after millions of striking workers brought Europe's fourth-largest economy to a standstill under the motto "Salaries. Housing. Prices" in the country's first general strike in 14 years earlier in the day.
The massive turnout came in response to housing shortages and unbearably high rents.
City officials in Barcelona said 55,000 people attended evening marches there as they walked behind a huge banner reading "Live. Not just survive." Housing activists in the city said the turnout was far larger, claiming that 400,000 had hit the streets.
As has been the case in other demonstrations across the Europea of late , peaceful protests later gave way to small groups of marauding young men who smashed storefront windows along Barcelona's main shopping street. They also set fire to dumpsters and shot fireworks at police when they arrived.
Earlier on Wednesday, workers across Spain gathered en masse, marching and setting up picket lines despite stormy weather in many areas of the country.
Symbolized by the eviction and death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid earlier this year, the crisis has also prompted a snap election set for November 29.
The government of left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez attempted to pass legislation to ease the plight of renters, but was blocked in parliament by opposition parties. Lacking the power to get legislation passed, Sanchez called the early vote in hopes of shoring up more support.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Sanchez's government did end up approving two extraordinary decrees introducing measures similar to the housing reforms rejected by parliament.
"We won't stop until we transform this country's housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the [landlord] minority," said Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union.
While most of the protests were peaceful, strikers in front of Madrid's Mercamadrid wholesale market said police had used pepper spray on the crowd, prompting at least 13 people to seek medical attention.
Some airlines later reported disruptions to flights in and out of Spain as some airport and airline workers participated in the strike.
The country has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set ​to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to estimates from the central bank.
With fewer and fewer individuals and families able to buy a home, the number of renters in the country has risen sharply. According to Spain's youth council, the average rent is €1,176 ($1,315). This is equivalent to 99% of the average young person's salary.
The general strike came a day after rail workers launched a strike over two major deadly train crashes this year, making decrepit infrastructure another major issue in the upcoming parliamentary elections.

Spain's government supported Wednesday's strike, saying it was staged "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition."
Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), had a different take, saying if it was indeed "a strike against the opposition," it was "an absurdity the likes of which does not exist in any other European Union country."
Although the UGT labor union — one of the strike organizers — and Sanchez's socialist PSOE party are two separate institutions, they share a historic founder in Pablo Iglesias Posse.

Here in Madrid, apparently, lots of people are still showing up for work, and people I know have clearly said they will not go on strike as they don't see much sense in it — although they all suffer under the cost of living crisis and the housing crisis.
There is also debate about this strike being an "election strike" that could benefit the current government.
"I'm not taking part in this. It's nonsense. The government is supporting it because they hope they'll get enough votes on the 29th so they can carry on," a doorman in Madrid told me.

articles.title_orig: Who could run Nvidia after Jensen Huang?
articles.title_zh: Who could run Nvidia after Jensen Huang?
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX founder and Tesla CEO Elon Musk said it would be "an honor" to hire embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , after reports emerged that Nvidia's board could be preparing to oust Huang from the company.
Late Wednesday stateside, financial blog Zerohedge wrote on X, "Elon please hire Jensen," to which Musk replied , "That would be an honor."
The post comes as the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia's board is preparing to meet as soon as Wednesday to discuss Huang's future at the company.
The report also followed a New York Times story that Huang had an extramarital relationship with another Nvidia executive. The developments sent Nvidia shares down more than 8% in after-hours trading.
Huang and Nvidia have dominated headlines since the weekend after the Nvidia CEO acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. intelligence identified as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security.
Alice Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, was recruited to gather information on Jensen, according to people briefed on the intelligence cited by The New York Times.
The Nvidia chief sought to project a "business as usual" atmosphere on his first day back at the office after the revelations, but he is now facing calls to resign from several lawmakers.
Sen. Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., a member of the Senate Banking Committee, reiterated Wednesday his call for Huang to resign, joining Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., a member of the House Oversight Committee and Rep. Don Bacon , R-Neb., who is retiring from Congress.
"As a matter of his own conscience, he should resign," Cramer told CNBC.

articles.title_orig: Iran Update, November 11, 2026
articles.title_zh: Iran Update, November 11, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
The US Department of Justice indicted three members of an Iranian-supported Kataib Hezbollah front group on November 10 for their involvement in nearly 20 attacks or plots in Europe and the United States, including an attempted attack on the Royal Air Force (RAF) base in Fairford in September 2026.[1] The three individuals conducted numerous attacks in Europe between March and May 2026 as part of the group known as Harakat Ashab al Yamin al Islamiya.[2] The Justice Department described Harakat Ashab al Yamin al Islamiya as a front group for Kataib Hezbollah and the IRGC.[3] Both Iran and the Iraqi militias have historically used front groups to provide plausible deniability and obfuscate their involvement in attacks and other activity.[4] The Justice Department indicted senior Kataib Hezbollah commander Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawoud al Saadi in May 2026 for his direction of Harakat Ashab al Yamin al Islamiya‘s attacks.[5] Saadi more recently organized the plot targeting RAF Fairford from prison in New York.[6] UK authorities thwarted a plot to attack US bombers stationed at the base with small explosive drones on September 27, which led the United States to relocate the bombers from the base.[7]
The front group’s pattern of activity suggests that its operations are part of an Iranian effort to compel Israel and the United States to halt attacks on Iran. The front group targeted and attempted to target numerous Jewish sites in Europe and the United States in March and April 2026, including synagogues.[8] The attacks likely aimed to retaliate against US-Israeli strikes in Iran by spreading terror and fear among US and European Jewish communities, thereby increasing the pressure on both countries to end the strike campaign. Such a strategy may reflect Iran’s recognition that previous direct Iranian attacks on Israeli soil failed to compel Israeli decisionmakers to avoid taking action against Iran.[9]
Limited US strikes on Iran in August and September, as well as reports that the United States was considering renewed strikes on Iran, may have motivated the cell’s shift from Jewish-affiliated targets to US military targets.[10]  The group paused attacks on any targets after Saadi was sentenced in the United States in May 2026. The Justice Department noted that the three men began to plan the RAF Fairford attack in August.[11] UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the House of Commons in mid-October that the IRGC ”almost certainly” directed the plot.[12] Attacks on US bases that support US operations, such as RAF Fairford, are likely intended to deter future US attacks on Iran. Iranian officials have increasingly issued threats against US bases in Europe amid expectations that the United States could imminently strike Iran again. Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei warned Arabic-language media on November 11 that Iran would target distant US bases in the event of any new attack, for example.[13] It is not clear if Rezaei is threatening to conduct direct missile or drone attacks against such bases or referring to sabotage. Several US bases in Europe lie within the range of Iran’s existing missiles.[14] The Wall Street Journal reported on November 10 that US forces relocated multiple tankers from the RAF Mildenhall Base to Germany and other countries due to an imminent threat from Iran, citing people familiar with the matter.[15]
Ansar al Furqan, a Baloch Salafi-jihadi group, has at least partially merged into the Mobarizoun Popular Front (MPF), a coalition of Baloch anti-regime groups that has conducted several operations in Sistan and Baluchistan Province in recent months.[16] The MPF claimed that the merger would unite Baloch armed groups and increase the effectiveness of anti-regime operations. [17] Jaish al Adl and several other Baloch militant groups formed the MPF in December 2025 to fight against the regime and increase coordination among anti-regime groups in southeastern Iran.[18] Ansar al Furqan did not publicly join the MPF when the coalition formed and continued to operate independently. MPF Spokesperson Mahmoud Baloch announced on November 11 that Ansar al Furqan had merged into the MPF after unspecified Baloch figures mediated between the groups.[19]  It is unclear at this time how fully Ansar al Furqan has merged into the MPF. An anti-regime Baloch media outlet subsequently reported that Ansar al Furqan spokesperson Molavi Nasrollah Baloch confirmed the full merger.[20] An alleged direct statement from Ansar al Furqan alternatively suggested that only a small number of its fighters chose to join the MPF on their own initiative and that Ansar al Furqan’s foundational structure and principal divisions remain intact.[21] The discrepancies in reporting about Ansar al Furqan‘s decision to join the MPF may reflect internal splits within the group, although available reporting does not identify the defectors or explain why they joined the MPF. This merger comes amid an uptick in anti-regime militant activity in southeastern Iran in recent months.[22]
Ansar al Furqan and the MPF share the common objective to overthrow the Iranian regime, which may explain in part Ansar al Furqan’s decision to join the MPF at this time. Ansar al Furqan called the MPF fighters its “brothers” and expressed support for their anti-regime struggle, which indicates that the groups share a common enemy despite their ideological differences.[23] The MPF’s charter identifies “deep political change” in Iran as its central objective and frames its struggle around the regime’s oppression of Baloch citizens and other Iranians.[24] The MPF has explicitly called for the overthrow of the Velayat-e Faqih [the Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist] system, but the coalition has not advocated for Baloch independence or autonomy.[25] The MPF contains Salafi-jihadi groups, such as Jaish al Adl, but the coalition itself has not expressed Salafi-jihadi views.  Ansar al Furqan also seeks the regime’s collapse but frames its campaign as jihad and emphasizes the role of religious scholars in its leadership.[26] Ansar al Furqan has used sectarian terms to refer to the Iranian regime and Shia groups, whereas the MPF promotes cooperation among Iranians across ideological divisions.[27]  Shared objectives to collapse the regime may have encouraged some fighters to join the MPF, while strict ideological adherence may have compelled other Ansar al Furqan fighters to remain independent. Ideological differences between Ansar al Furqan and the MPF could lead to disagreements over rhetoric, recruitment, or ideology that could limit the feasibility of the partnership.
The Ansar al Furqan fighters who joined the MPF may increase the coalition’s capabilities through additional manpower and combat experience. It is unclear how many Ansar al Furqan fighters have joined the MPF, however. Ansar al Furqan has conducted some tactically sophisticated attacks, including a large-scale attack against a Law Enforcement Command (LEC) checkpoint in Fahraj, Kerman Province, in December 2025.[28] The MPF has already demonstrated the ability to conduct complex operations across southeastern Iran, including a nine-hour engagement in Saravan in September and a combined improvised explosive device (IED) and small-arms attack in Jalgh in October.[29]  The impacts of Ansar al Furqan’s merger on the MPF’s capabilities will also depend on the extent to which the MPF incorporates these fighters into the MPF’s command structures.
Nothing significant to report.

Nothing

articles.title_orig: Indonesia’s vice president resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned
articles.title_zh: Indonesia’s vice president resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned
articles.content_orig:
Indonesia's vice-president resigned Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.
Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former president Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.
Raka had offered to resign Tuesday during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy. But a Cabinet minister said the president urged Raka at the time to defend himself and it wasn't clear if he accepted the resignation offer.
The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.
A subsequent petition, submitted Wednesday to the House leadership by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties, began a parliamentary process that could lead to his impeachment.
Under Indonesian law, House leaders must establish a special committee to examine whether Raka has violated the constitution by serving as vice president, despite allegedly failing to meet election requirements.
If lawmakers determine there is sufficient basis for the accusation, the House must ask the Constitutional Court to rule on whether a constitutional violation has occurred.
The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent challenged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to label Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat in a Situation Room confrontation last week that illustrates the tension inside the Trump administration over Chinese access to Nvidia’s advanced chips, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks. But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, also were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who the intelligence community suspected of being a Chinese spy, people familiar with the matter said.
But despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, the people said.
Confronted on it by Bessent last Thursday, Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said.
Axios first reported the Situation Room confrontation.
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that was originally incorporated in 2015 as a Chinese video game developer called 7Road International. But in the three years since Alice Huang became director and the company changed its name, it has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia , purchasing more than $4 billion worth of its semiconductors, by some analyst estimates.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and said it is a “compliant and legal company.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”
The entity list represents one of the US’s most significant tools for preventing American firms from selling their products to foreign companies and organizations. But adding Megaspeed to the list could also risk inflaming tensions with China amid Trump’s efforts to manage the US’ trade relationship with the fellow superpower. The Commerce Department hasn’t added any company to the list in more than a year.
Representatives for the Treasury and Commerce departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: Giant statue of Roman emperor once stood in southern Scotland
articles.title_zh: Giant statue of Roman emperor once stood in southern Scotland
articles.content_orig:
A giant gilded statue of a Roman emperor once stood proudly in the heart of the Scottish Borders, new research suggests.
It had previously been assumed that a bronze leg found in a bog in Milsington near Hawick in 1820 was loot taken from a site further south - possibly York.
However, experts now believe it came from a sculpture of Antoninus Pius on horseback - similar to the one of his successor Marcus Aurelius in Rome - and was erected to mark the conquest of southern Scotland.
Dr Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland (NMS), said: "This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland."
The sculpture is the only known example of its kind from Scotland and has been reconstructed using its surviving leg ahead of a major new exhibition opening at NMS in Edinburgh this weekend.
The larger than life-sized lower leg with a boot dates back to about AD140 and is one of the most striking treasures from Roman Britain in the NMS collection.
A wider study of statue fragments from the Roman frontier showed that bronze imperial statues - including equestrian ones - were erected in frontier forts, thus making a Scottish location for this particular statue more feasible.
In addition, researchers said the way the leg was removed suggested the deliberate Roman dismantling of a valued sculpture as they withdrew from southern Scotland, rather than a local act of revenge.
They said it had been carefully removed, not "brutally hacked off".
Examination of the top of the leg has found that there are no cut marks, but rather it remains exactly as it was cast.
The absence of gilding around the knee shows that this area was covered by a tunic or cloak, with lumps around the top which in-filled the folds of the tunic and stuck the leg to it.
This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap, typically resulting in irregular fragments on a much smaller scale.
Such careful removal and burial has been found widely in Roman Scotland when the Antonine conquests were abandoned. Examples include the burial of Antonine Wall inscriptions and the Inveresk Mithras altars, which are also on display in the exhibition.
Once curators had established that the statue was likely to have been erected in Scotland, they looked to answer the question of who it depicted.
They came to the conclusion that just one emperor paid particular heed to his Scottish victories - Antoninus Pius.
His conquest of what is now southern Scotland was the only foreign adventure that he commemorated with the title Imperator, a battle-honour meaning "commander" which marked an emperor's victory.
Hunter said: "This was a big deal for the emperor, something which was worth celebrating.
"It offers us a tantalising glimpse into the kind of grand monuments which once stood in southern Scotland and shows the importance Pius placed on his victories in Scotland.
"But it begs the question - where is the rest of the statue?".
Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire is at NMS in Edinburgh from 14 November to 18 April.
Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor for more than two decades, from AD 138 to 161.
He has been described as "mild-mannered and capable" and was the fourth of the "five good emperors" who guided the empire through an 84-year period of "internal peace and prosperity".
He succeeded Hadrian and it was during his reign that a 36-mile (58km) garrisoned barrier - the Antonine Wall - was built to extend the Roman frontier 100 miles (160km) north of Hadrian's Wall.
After his death, the empire suffered invasion by hostile tribes and civil unrest.
