articles.title_orig: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
articles.title_zh: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
articles.content_orig:
The US has proposed that Russia prepare a new draft security agreement with Europe, in which Moscow would outline not only its demands but also the steps it is prepared to take to reduce tensions.
Source: Axios , citing two sources familiar with the matter
Details: For many years, Russia has sought to conclude a European security agreement that would restrict NATO enlargement and reduce the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe. The US has rejected these demands in the past but now appears willing to consider them in some form as part of a wider agreement to end the war in Ukraine.
However, the governments of many European countries are deeply suspicious of the administration's approach.
US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will meet with Russian leader Vladimir Putin in Moscow on 12 November to reiterate this demand. They also want Putin to consent to the participation of European representatives in the next round of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, a US official said.
The US proposal for an agreement on a new security architecture between Europe and Russia as part of a deal to end the war in Ukraine was a key topic of the talks in Abu Dhabi.
Russian negotiators said Putin had launched the invasion of Ukraine because then-US president Joe Biden had not responded to his 2021 letter outlining his security concerns, according to two sources familiar with the talks.
One source said Kushner and Witkoff had told the Russians that the world had changed significantly since 2021.
They proposed that Russia prepare a new draft agreement that would address its security concerns and demands but also specify what "symmetrical steps" it was prepared to take to de-escalate the conflict and reassure Europe that it would not attack in the future.
Kushner and Witkoff also told the Russians that, for serious discussions on European security to take place, they would have to agree to the participation of European representatives in future peace talks.
So far, Russia has been unwilling to allow Europeans to participate in peace talks with Ukraine.
The US hopes that giving European representatives a seat at the peace talks will make their governments more willing to discuss and conclude a broader security agreement even before the war ends.
"Zelenskyy won't agree to a deal until he knows what happens next regarding security guarantees and Putin wants to know this, too. This is why the security issue is so important," the source said.
The source added that the US had made it clear to European countries that it would not agree to a security deal with Russia unless Europe and Ukraine were involved. The US would also not give Russia veto power over European security matters, the source said.

articles.title_orig: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 11, 2026
articles.title_zh: Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, November 11, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
Senior Kremlin officials explicitly and emphatically articulated Moscow’s persistent demands for complete Ukrainian capitulation and territorial concessions that extend far beyond Donbas . Vladimir Medinsky, Russian presidential aide and head of the Russian delegation at Abu Dhabi, told Russian media outlets on November 11 that Russia will capture “every inch of [Russia’s] land one way or another.”[1] Medinsky also asserted that “wherever a Russian soldier has set foot belongs to Russia” — mirroring Russian President Vladimir Putin’s statement from June 2025.[2] Medinsky added that Russia will not accept any territorial exchanges with Ukraine and will continue to expand its “security zone” in Ukraine (very likely referring to territory in northern Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts that Russian officials claim are part of a “buffer zone.”).[3] Medinsky’s statements demonstrate the Kremlin’s territorial ambitions beyond the five illegally annexed regions in Ukraine (Crimea and Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts) and unwillingness to engage in compromises or exchanges of territory to end the war.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov similarly stated on November 11 that Russia will pursue a “course” that fulfills the demands Putin laid out in his June 2024 speech to the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA).[4] That speech required a Ukrainian withdrawal from the entirety of Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts, including areas that Russian forces have never occupied; Ukraine’s demilitarization and “denazification” (the replacement of the current Ukrainian government with a pro-Russian one); and Ukraine’s abandonment of its NATO aspirations.[5] Kremlin officials have frequently claimed that the Ukrainian withdrawal from all of Donetsk Oblast is a necessary but insufficient condition for a peace settlement , and Putin and other high-ranking Kremlin officials have often reiterated Russia’s commitment to Putin’s June 2024 demands.[6] Ukrainian forces maintain control over 0.38 percent of Luhansk Oblast, 20.12 percent of Donetsk Oblast, 24.42 percent of Zaporizhia Oblast, and 30.11 percent of Kherson Oblast, but Putin continues to demand territory that his forces have been unable to seize.[7]
Russian officials used the Abu Dhabi talks to try to persuade US and Ukrainian officials to accept Russia’s carefully crafted fictional version of the frontline. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated on November 10 that Russian military and intelligence officials falsely claimed to the US and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi that Russian forces control half of the part of Donbas that Ukrainian forces, in reality, still control.[8] The Kremlin has long made exaggerated and grossly inaccurate claims of Russian battlefield successes.[9] The Russian MoD, in fact, regularly claims a frontline trace that does not correspond with reality at all. The Russian MoD falsely claimed the seizure of Dobropillya and Oleksiievo-Druzhkivka on October 16, for example, when Russian forces held neither settlement.[10] Putin claimed on July 3 that Russian forces had seized Kostyantynivka — a town that Russian forces have still not seized over four months later.[11] The Russian MoD repeatedly falsely claimed that Russian forces encircled Ukrainian troops in northern Kharkiv Oblast in September and October 2026.[12] Russian state media regularly publishes maps showing the fictional Russian line of claimed advances.
The Kremlin will likely continue to make false claims of advances all along the frontline in an effort to establish its fictional frontline as the basis of future negotiations on territorial issues. Russian officials often claim that peace talks need to take into consideration the “realities on the ground,” and the Kremlin is trying to push its own reality onto US, Ukrainian, and other negotiators. The Kremlin will very likely increase its claimed advances throughout Winter 2026-2027 and into Spring 2027 far beyond territories its troops can take or hold. Putin likely hopes that a devastating wintertime Russian long-range strike campaign against Ukraine will break Ukraine’s will to continue to fight and degrade Western support for Ukraine, allowing him to insist on his claimed line of advance as the starting point of any talks about a final settlement of the war.
Ukrainian and US officials in Abu Dhabi reportedly rejected Russian officials’ false claims about the battlefield, and ample evidence of Ukrainian successes in 2026 directly undermines Russia’s false narrative. Zelensky stated on November 11 that US negotiators confirmed Ukraine’s assessment of the battlefield situation — rejecting the false Russian claim that Russian forces control half of the Ukrainian-controlled territory in Donbas.[13] Russian forces have, in fact, lost the initiative and much of their offensive capabilities in several sectors of the theater throughout 2026. Russian forces have suffered a net loss of territory in four of the last eight months since the previous round of US-Ukrainian-Russian talks in February 2026, while simultaneously suffering increasingly high casualties.[14] Ukrainian forces have conducted several successful counteroffensive operations throughout 2026 in the Lyman, Oleksandrivka, and Kupyansk directions, liberating over 1,000 square kilometers of territory. Successful Ukrainian counteroffensive operations have entirely disrupted the Russian plan to seize Donetsk Oblast and created cascading effects across other sectors of the frontline, as the Russian military command had to make difficult decisions about the allocation of manpower and resources between sectors.[15] There is no basis to assess that Russian forces will be able to take the rest of Donetsk Oblast in any short period of time, as Putin continues to claim that they will, or even to forecast that Russian forces will ever be able to seize the region by force.[16]
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the Abu Dhabi talks reportedly agreed to a large-scale prisoner of war (POW) exchange. Former Senior Advisor to the US President Jared Kushner reported on November 11 that Ukrainian and Russian officials agreed to a large-scale POW exchange but noted that the parties will finalize the numbers on November 12.[17] Zelensky reported on November 11 that the delegations discussed the possibility of each side exchanging 1,000 or 1,500 POWs.[18] Russian First Deputy Chief of Information of the General Staff’s Main Directorate (GRU) Lieutenant General Alexander Zorin stated that an exchange of 1,000 POWs could take place in the next two to three weeks (around November 25 to December 2).[19] Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada (Parliament) Deputy Davyd Arakhamia stated that this POW exchange could be ”one of the biggest, if not the biggest” of the war.[20]
The US delegation will meet with Putin in Moscow City on November 12 to discuss the progress of the talks and the potential involvement of European officials in future negotiations, while the Kremlin continues to explicitly reject the idea of a multilateral format. Kushner stated on November 11 that he and US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff will next travel to Moscow to meet with Putin in an attempt to make further progress on peace talks and to promote the idea of future European participation.[21] Kremlin Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stated on November 11, however, that Russian officials currently have “no vision” of a negotiations format that includes European representatives —echoing repeated Kremlin statements in recent weeks against European involvement.[22] Kushner noted that the US delegation will also travel to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Zelensky following the visit to Moscow.[23]
The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs reported that Alexander Darchiev, the Russian ambassador to the United States, passed away on November 11 at the age of 66. [24] Darchiev had served as ambassador since March 6,

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Chinese AI firms rush to secure Nvidia chip capacity as spy scandal stirs fear of US curbs
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Chinese AI firms rush to secure Nvidia chip capacity as spy scandal stirs fear of US curbs
articles.content_orig:
A House-passed bill would give the Commerce Department authority over cloud access to restricted chips, which Chinese firms rent abroad
Some Chinese AI companies have contacted overseas data-center operators about reserving Nvidia $NVDA chip capacity, according to Reuters , amid concern that the controversy around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could lead Washington to restrict cloud-based access to advanced processors.
U.S. export controls keep Nvidia 's top-end AI processors out of China, yet Chinese firms can still lease them in data centers located abroad. One of China's large cloud providers has held internal talks about reserving capacity abroad, according to Reuters. Smaller AI developers are mulling comparable moves, such as reaching out to compute-rental firms in Southeast Asia.
The companies worry the episode will build support for the Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, a bill that would empower the Commerce Department to oversee how restricted technology is accessed through the cloud, according to Reuters. The House approved the measure in January on a 369-22 vote, but the Senate has yet to act on it.
Jensen Huang acknowledged on Sunday, Nov. 8, that he had cheated on his wife. The woman in question was Alice Huang, who previously worked as an executive at Megaspeed, a cloud company based in Singapore, and U.S. authorities determined she was operating as an intelligence asset for China, according to The New York Times . The two Huangs are unrelated, and China has denied the allegation, according to Reuters.
Megaspeed has rejected claims that it illegally sent chips to China, according to Reuters, following U.S. investigators' scrutiny of whether it aided Chinese clients in getting hold of export-controlled Nvidia chips. The company said Thursday that it had assisted inspectors from the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security and engaged a U.S. law firm to catalog its graphics processing units.
Shares of Alibaba, Z.ai and MiniMax fell in Hong Kong on Thursday. Alibaba shed up to 7.1% at its low point, and the other two each lost 7% or more.
Traders and intermediaries in China’s gray market have started stockpiling restricted Nvidia chips, according to Reuters. The Commerce Department is finalizing a rule meant to stop Chinese AI firms from getting at advanced chips via overseas data centers, according to CNBC , which cited The Information. Lawmakers are pushing to add chip-control bills to this year’s National Defense Authorization Act, CNBC said.
Chinese AI firms including Moonshot AI, ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have been reported to have obtained access to restricted Nvidia chips through data centers in Thailand, Malaysia, Japan and elsewhere in Asia . U.S. export controls cover the physical transfer of chips but not remote access to them, said Cassia King, a senior researcher in the Compute Policy group at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy.
RASA alone would fall short of closing the loophole, said Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow in technology and national security at the Center for a New American Security. The bill would establish legal authority to regulate remote access, she said, but a separate rulemaking process would be required before that authority could be used on advanced chips.

articles.title_orig: United Airlines flight emergency: Unruly passenger hospitalized after being removed from plane from Tokyo, Japan to Chicago O'Hare
articles.title_zh: United Airlines flight emergency: Unruly passenger hospitalized after being removed from plane from Tokyo, Japan to Chicago O'Hare
articles.content_orig:
A United Airlines flight was met by a medical crew and law enforcement upon its landing at Chicago O'Hare International Airport on Wednesday afternoon. The flight departed from Tokyo and experienced a level 3 emergency , which the flight crew confirmed to air traffic controllers.
According to early reports, the unruly passenger on the flight was contained with flex cuffs . Upon landing in Chicago , the unruly passenger was taken to the hospital for further evaluation . At this time, there are no reports of further injuries to passengers or crew members.
The incident was one of two major issues at O'Hare Airport on Wednesday, as another flight also diverted to the airport over a bathroom leak.
A United Airlines passenger on flight 868 was taken to hospital upon arrival at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD). The flight from Haneda Airport (HND) declared an emergency onboard due to the unruly passenger on Wednesday afternoon. ​​​​​​​The flight arrived on time without delays at 2:39 p.m. local time at Terminal 5 in Chicago. ​​​​​​​
The flight crew declared a Level 3 emergency onboard. Level 1 emergencies typically consist of disruptive behavior, while Level 2 emergencies are linked to physical and abusive behavior.
As for this Level 3 warning, it typically involves life-threatening behavior, including the passenger possessing a weapon, sabotage of the aircraft system, or other life-threatening attacks that may be physical. A Level 4 emergency is the highest threat involving a flight deck breach.
In this instance, on flight 868, the passenger clearly violated United Airlines' contract of carriage rules by failing to obey commands.
The airline writes in its contract of carriage, "Whenever refusal or removal of a Passenger may be necessary for the safety of such Passenger or other Passengers or members of the crew including, but not limited to: Passengers who fail to comply with or interfere with the duties of the members of the flight crew, federal regulations, or security directives. Or, passengers who assault any employee of UA, including the gate agents and flight crew, any employees of carriers doing business as United Express, any UA or United Express vendor employee, or any UA Passenger."
Despite a potential diversion due to the incident, the flight reached its destination. The unruly passenger was brought to the hospital upon landing for further evaluation.
According to audio posted regarding the incident, the unruly passenger was "restrained with flex cuffs" on the flight. It has not been confirmed how the unruly passenger was put in the flex cuffs, or if other United customers assisted the crew in restraining the individual.
There were no law enforcement officials on board.
The United Airlines crew also confirmed the threat level classification during their conversation with air traffic controllers. In response, the ground controllers confirmed that, along with a medical team, law enforcement would also meet the flight.
"I believe they're still on their way," the controllers said after law enforcement confirmed they would meet the flight.
No further information is available about the incident. TheTravel has contacted United Airlines for a statement regarding the unruly passenger on flight 868.
In addition, a Frontier Airlines flight from Denver International Airport (DEN) to Detroit Metro Airport (DTW) was forced to make an emergency landing at O'Hare Airport on Wednesday. The diversion occurred because of a rare bathroom issue. According to reports, flight 3566 changed course because a bathroom faucet caused water to flow onto the aircraft floor.
Additionally, two private planes made contact at Chicago Midway Airport, causing a minor runway disruption.
According to FlightAware , Chicago O'Hare Airport had 706 delays on Wednesday, the highest number of any U.S. airport. United Airlines accounted for 141 delays, 20% of its flight total out of Chicago. The airport had seven cancelled flights.

articles.title_orig: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
articles.title_zh: Critical Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Could Let Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code Remotely
articles.content_orig:
A critical flaw in Apache HTTP Server's HTTP/2 module, mod_http2 , can let a remote attacker run code on the server. Tracked as CVE-2026-119618 , it affects versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 and is fixed in version 2.4.71, released yesterday.
Only servers with HTTP/2 enabled are affected, according to Red Hat, which ships the server as part of Red Hat Enterprise Linux.
An attacker who can reach the server needs no authentication to exploit the flaw and could take full control of the server process, the Linux vendor says. It rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale.
The vendor's assessment, published yesterday, also says "public research has demonstrated a reliable exploit" against a server in its default configuration with mod_http2 enabled. It does not name or link that research. Security company Wiz said later that day that no exploit was available and that no exploitation in the wild had been reported.
HTTP/2 runs only where the Protocols directive turns it on, as the module documentation explains. The directive uses h2 for HTTP/2 over TLS and h2c for HTTP/2 over plain TCP. It can be set for the whole server or for a single virtual host, so admins should check the server-wide setting and every virtual host.
Standalone builds of the module, released on GitHub as mod_h2, are affected from version 2.0.8 through 2.0.42.
Admins who run the Apache HTTP Server project's own releases should move to version 2.4.71, the fixed release named in its security advisory . That release also fixes a crash in mod_md, rated important, and a one-byte overwrite of stack memory in mod_vhost_alias, rated low.
The distributions in the table below ship their own builds of the server, with their own package version numbers. On Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9, for example, the fix ships as mod_http2-2.0.26-7.el9_9.1.
Red Hat shipped fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10 yesterday and rates the flaw Important on those releases rather than Critical. Their mod_http2 packages give each HTTP/2 stream its own memory allocator, which makes an attack much harder, according to the vendor's severity assessment . Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and earlier do not contain the vulnerable code.
The Debian rows come from Debian's security tracker , and the Amazon row from the Amazon Linux tracker . Ubuntu's CVE tracker had no page for the flaw when The Hacker News checked it today.
The Apache HTTP Server advisory offers no workaround. In its vulnerability analysis , Wiz advises admins who cannot update yet to remove h2 and h2c from the Protocols directive, leaving Protocols http/1.1.
The standalone mod_h2 project has published no fixed release so far. Its release list on GitHub ends at 2.0.42, the last affected version, and its repository has been read-only since it was archived on June 9. The Protocols change above also applies to servers that use those builds.
The flaw was reported on October 26 by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, a free scanning service for open-source projects that uses the company's AI models. Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported it last week.
An earlier HTTP/2 flaw , CVE-2026-23918, was fixed in version 2.4.67, released on May 4. Servers updated to that release, or to any later one up to 2.4.70, still run a version that the new flaw affects.

articles.title_orig: Chinese firms can boost valuation using buy-backs, payouts: Goldman Sachs
articles.title_zh: Chinese firms can boost valuation using buy-backs, payouts: Goldman Sachs
articles.content_orig:
Share issuance has diluted the market and impacted investors’ returns, the US bank says
Chinese companies could unlock a further 15 per cent in equity valuation upside by stepping up share buy-backs and dividend payouts, as Beijing seeks to encourage listed firms to return more cash to investors, according to Goldman Sachs.
The US investment bank said in a report on Wednesday that an increase in corporate payout ratios and share repurchases, in line with policymakers’ efforts to improve shareholder returns, could lift valuations of the MSCI China Index by about 15 per cent from current levels through improved returns on equity and cash distributions to shareholders.
Goldman said Chinese companies had historically favoured issuing new shares over buying them back, with equity issuance outpacing repurchases for most of the past two decades.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Tumbles as Investors Consider Future Without CEO Huang
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Tumbles as Investors Consider Future Without CEO Huang
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's board of directors is preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang soon, according to two sources familiar with the matter, following allegations that Huang had an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies believe was a Chinese asset.
The Trump administration is aware of the matter, the sources said.
The Wall Street Journal was first to report on the board's moves.
Nvidia's share price slid more than 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday after the Journal's report, extending a multi-day sell-off for one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies.
The company has faced days of turmoil following reports that American intelligence agencies believed Huang was the target of a Chinese spying plot.
Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993, and for years it was best known for designing graphics cards widely used for gaming. The company now designs the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
The New York Times reported last week on allegations that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who previously led a Singapore-based firm called Megaspeed International that bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips and hardware. U.S. intelligence agencies have believed for months that Alice Huang — who is not related to Jensen Huang — was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, the newspaper reported.
In a message to Nvidia employees over the weekend, Jensen Huang wrote that he was "unfaithful to my wife" and apologized for hurting her and their children. He did not name the woman involved.
Nvidia's board said Sunday it had launched an independent investigation into allegations that the CEO "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."
Two law enforcement sources told CBS News the Justice Department is also investigating Megaspeed over potential violations of U.S. export restrictions on advanced AI chips. Some analysts have raised questions about whether the saga resulted in China — which is racing the U.S. for AI dominance — gaining access to Nvidia's technology through Megaspeed. The company has denied any involvement in illegal chip transfers.
China has denied all allegations, with Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun telling reporters on Monday that the "so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."
Beyond the national security concerns, Nvidia is facing a securities lawsuit accusing the company of failing to disclose information to shareholders about Jensen Huang's relationship with the alleged spy.
Jensen Huang has a close relationship with the Trump administration. President Trump gave Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 computer chips to "approved customers" in China late last year, with the federal government taking a 25% cut of chip sales. The deal did not include Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell or Rubin systems.
The Nvidia CEO and other U.S. tech executives traveled to China with Mr. Trump earlier this year.
On Monday, Mr. Trump called Jensen Huang a "very high-quality person," saying during a White House briefing that "the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." The president said he spoke to Jensen Huang to see how he was doing, and the executive "said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."

articles.title_orig: Senior US Democratic senators urge administration to preserve Nvidia export records amid China security concerns
articles.title_zh: Senior US Democratic senators urge administration to preserve Nvidia export records amid China security concerns
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration has briefed top lawmakers on a growing national security crisis around the world’s leading chipmaker, Nvidia, after its chief executive, Jensen Huang, admitted over the weekend to an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy .
Senior U.S. intelligence officials briefed the Gang of Eight — congressional leaders from both parties, and the chairs and vice chairs of the House and Senate intelligence committees — on the matter, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Monday.
Congressional Republicans have called on Huang himself to provide an update, warning the incident raised “significant national security concerns” that could have compromised cutting-edge American technology at a critical moment in the race with China for supremacy in artificial intelligence.
Huang admitted Sunday to having an affair with Alice Huang, who was identified as a Chinese intelligence asset by U.S. authorities, after the New York Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had raised concerns within the administration about his potential compromise.
Nvidia’s board of directors said Sunday it will launch an investigation into its CEO Jensen Huang, after he revealed he had an affair with a former Chinese executive.
President Trump is scheduled to visit China next week.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Jensen Huang said in a statement Sunday.
“Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports,” he added, “NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company, and I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”
Debate over export controls for the world’s most advanced semiconductor chips, produced by Nvidia, has raged over the last eight years in Washington, with lawmakers across party lines expressing concern that Chinese access to the chips could strengthen their hand in the development of the most powerful AI models.
Huang has been one of the most vocal opponents of the U.S. export controls, calling them a “mistake” and saying they were hurting American businesses more than they were constricting Chinese government efforts.
The executive was successful in lobbying the Trump administration to ease export restrictions on some of Nvidia’s most advanced chips over the past year.
Jeffries said he would be calling for greater export controls on chips after the incident. The New York congressman is expected to become the next speaker of the House after Democrats swept into power in this month’s midterm elections.
“We’re going to need a full briefing specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue,” Jeffries said, adding that “real concerns” have arisen from the case that will need to be addressed.
U.S. intelligence unmasked the Chinese intelligence operation after intercepting the communications of Alice Huang, a former journalist with Chinese state media who later became a senior executive at Megaspeed International. The Singaporean data center firm was already under the microscope for allegedly funneling restricted AI chips to Beijing.
Trump was reportedly made aware of the Chinese espionage effort targeting Huang, but chose not to act, according to the New York Times.
Nvidia’s stock dropped more than 4% Monday , after the board said it would open an investigation into its chief executive  being the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
The company “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” it said in the statement.
Some of the world’s leading financiers are sounding increasingly alarmed about an AI bubble.
“While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” it continued. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Rubio declined to address questions from reporters on the matter Monday.
“It’s an internal corporate matter for them, so I’m just not going to comment on that topic,” the secretary of State and national security advisor said.
But the administration could face increased calls to investigate Jensen Huang, a Trump ally, who traveled with Trump to Beijing in May and attended a state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September held at the White House.
Republicans have also formally requested Huang appear before the House on Nov. 18 — when Trump will be in China — to brief them on what happened.
Rep. Brian Mast of Florida, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Rick Crawford of Arkansas, head of the House Intelligence Committee, and Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, who leads the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said the issue of Chinese infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology “is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress.”
“It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” they wrote.

articles.title_orig: The world's super-rich are piling into alternative investments. Here's why
articles.title_zh: The world's super-rich are piling into alternative investments. Here's why
articles.content_orig:
The world's wealthiest investors are increasingly looking beyond stocks and bonds, pouring money into hedge funds, private equity and infrastructure assets, as market volatility and fears about stubborn inflation spur diversification.
From Asian billionaires to global family offices, alternative investments are becoming a bigger part of portfolios once dominated by traditional assets, said industry watchers
JPMorgan Asset Management's private wealth alternative assets in Asia-Pacific surged 40% over the past 12 months, according to Dan Watkins, the firm's regional chief executive officer, underscoring the growing appetite among high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients.
"So you really have this huge appetite for alternative exposure happening in that ultra-high-net-worth, high-net-worth category," Watkins said recently at a media summit in Singapore.
The shift comes as investors grapple with increasingly concentrated equity markets, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns that stocks and bonds may not provide the same protection against market downturns as they once did, experts said.
"We are seeing a sharp increase in planned asset allocation to alternatives among the family offices we speak to," said John Woods, chief investment officer for Asia at Lombard Odier.
Alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios, surpassing traditional assets for the first time, according to BNY Wealth . Traditional assets accounted for 41% of allocations, the report found.
Wealthy investors are seeking diversification, income and access to investments outside listed markets, and concerns over elevated valuations, tight credit spreads and the growing correlation between stocks and bonds have accelerated the trend, Woods added.
Hedge funds are emerging as a favored option among wealthy investors seeking protection against market swings, particularly as traditional diversification strategies face growing challenges.
Olaolu Aganga, head of portfolio construction and analytics at Citi Wealth, said hedge funds have attracted the strongest recent interest among qualified clients, who are seeking returns less dependent on the direction of equity markets.
Private credit is another area drawing interest, offering investors contractual income streams, while some hedge fund strategies seek to profit from differences in performance between companies rather than relying on broad market rallies, said Woods.
Citi's 2026 survey of 351 family offices found that inflation was their biggest concern, followed by interest rates, financial system stability and market volatility.
Wealthy families are increasingly seeking investments that can generate income and help preserve purchasing power amid persistent inflation and interest-rate uncertainty, while diversifying portfolios against market volatility, according to Aganga.
The Citi survey, however, also showed public equities recorded the strongest net increase in allocations, suggesting wealthy investors are adding alternatives rather than abandoning traditional markets. "This is not a wholesale rotation away from public markets," Woods said.
Infrastructure has emerged as another major beneficiary of the shift, with the artificial intelligence boom creating enormous demand for data centers, electricity networks and digital connectivity.
Thomas Roland Guyot, head of private markets investment specialists for Southeast Asia at UBS Unified Global Alternatives, said investors are increasingly targeting assets that support AI, electrification and energy security.
Such investments potentially offer a combination of long-term growth and relatively predictable cash flows, particularly where revenues are supported by essential demand or long-term contracts.
Investor appetite is already showing up in fund flows. Net inflows into open-ended infrastructure funds rose 30% year on year in the 12 months through the first quarter of 2026, according to PitchBook data cited by UBS.
Private equity remains a cornerstone of wealthy investors' alternative portfolios, although they are becoming more selective. Family offices are increasingly favoring direct investments in companies, co-investments alongside private equity managers and purchases of existing fund stakes on the secondary market, rather than relying solely on traditional pooled funds, according to Citi Wealth's Aganga.
Such approaches can give investors greater control over their investments or opportunities to acquire assets at discounts, said Lombard Odier's Woods.
The broader shift is also being facilitated by the growth of evergreen and semi-liquid funds, which have lowered minimum investment thresholds and reduced some administrative hurdles associated with traditional private-market funds, Woods added.
Investing into alternative assets does not come without risks, even as mitigating those is driving flows.
Private investments can lock up capital for years, while valuations may be slow to reflect deteriorating market conditions. Even funds marketed as semi-liquid can restrict withdrawals when redemption requests surge.
"Improved access does not equal liquidity," JPMorgan's Watkins said.
Citi's Aganga also warned that performance can vary significantly between managers, while private assets may appear less volatile than they actually are because valuations are updated less frequently.
Investors must also guard against unintended concentration. A portfolio holding data centers through real estate, infrastructure and private equity funds may appear diversified while remaining heavily exposed to the same AI investment cycle, UBS' Guyot said.
For now, the flow of capital into alternative assets shows their increasing appeal among the rich, though not at the expense of traditional investment, with Woods pointing out that much of the new investment is being funded by fresh capital and excess cash rather than large-scale sales of stocks and bonds.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | U.S. Aircraft Evacuated From Second U.K. Base Due to Iran Threat

articles.content_orig:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday after the G7 Foreign Ministers' meeting in Paris, that "bad things are happening to the Iranian economy and it's unfortunate."
The U.S. Air Force abruptly relocated more than a dozen aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England amid an emerging security threat, U.S. officials confirmed Tuesday.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the move, citing sources who said the threat originated in Iran.
As U.S. officials assessed the threat's nature and urgency, commanders raised the base's security level to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the military's second-highest alert level, indicating a likely terrorist threat against personnel or facilities.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
U.S. Air Force KC-135, used for in-flight refueling, takes off from RAF Mildenhall Airbase. (AP Photo/Max Nash, File)
Flight-tracking data and open-source analysts with the Military Air Tracking Alliance identified 13 U.S. aircraft leaving the base late Monday, the Associated Press said.
Nine Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers were moved to airfields in Scotland, Germany and Spain.
Three CV-22B Ospreys were relocated to nearby RAF Lakenheath, which has hardened aircraft shelters.
A U.S. official told The Associated Press the moves were precautionary, noting that some aircraft were on rotational deployments while others were permanently stationed in the United Kingdom .
IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY
American aircrews check a B-52 Stratofortress long-range subsonic bomber aircraft on the pan at RAF Fairford. The United Kingdom reportedly is refusing to let the United States use the base for a potential attack on Iran. (Getty Images)
The move marks the second major relocation of U.S. military aircraft from Britain in less than two months.
In early October, the Air Force pulled heavy bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire after British counterterrorism police stopped three suspicious vans headed toward the base Sept. 27.
Two men have since been charged under the United Kingdom's National Security Act.
Separately, the Justice Department unsealed indictments against three Iranian-backed operatives on Tuesday accused of involvement in coordinated terrorist plots across Europe, including RAF Fairford.
UK POLICE ARREST 'EXPLOSIVE' SUSPECTS NEAR US AIRBASE, KEY TO IRAN WAR
The main gate of RAF Fairford is pictured on September 27, 2026 in Fairford, United Kingdom. Police declared a major incident after evacuating residents from their homes in Whelford, a village about one mile from RAF Fairford, a military base that hosts U.S. Air Force bombers involved in the Iran conflict. (David Bown/Getty Images)
RAF Mildenhall is home to the 100th Air Refueling Wing, the only permanently based U.S. tanker wing in Europe.
Its KC-135 Stratotankers support allied aerial refueling and long-range strike missions across the region.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Washington routinely repositions military forces.
"We are constantly repositioning forces around the world for a variety of reasons," Rubio told reporters when asked about the evacuation.

A 10 Downing Street spokesperson said British air bases remain secure and that London and Washington continuously share intelligence on potential threats.

articles.title_orig: ‘Trump and His Envoys Are Working for Putin, Not the US,’ Democrats Warn
articles.title_zh: ‘Trump and His Envoys Are Working for Putin, Not the US,’ Democrats Warn
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Top congressional Democrats sharply condemn Trump, Kushner, and Witkoff for undermining Ukraine, pressuring Kyiv to surrender sovereign territory, and promoting Kremlin demands that threaten NATO and US national security.
Three senior US Democratic lawmakers sharply condemned President Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Wednesday, Nov. 11, accusing them of undermining Ukraine’s ability to resist Russia’s invasion, pressuring Kyiv to surrender sovereign territory, and promoting Kremlin demands that threaten NATO and US national security.
In a strongly worded joint statement, Congressman Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee; Congressman Adam Smith, ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee; and Senator Jack Reed, ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, sharply condemned the envoys for undermining Ukraine while advancing Russian interests.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“Ukraine continues to inflict massive casualties on the Russian Army and cripple the Russian economy, while US Special Envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff continue to undermine Ukraine’s ability to negotiate a just and lasting settlement in Putin’s brutal and illegal invasion,” the lawmakers said.
They also warned that the envoys’ actions threatened NATO, which they described as “the most successful alliance in history.”
“Their parroting of Kremlin talking points on renegotiating European security and possibly pulling back from Eastern Europe is totally unacceptable to the continued viability of NATO and the national security of the US,” the statement said.
The lawmakers accused Kushner and Witkoff of repeatedly pressuring Kyiv to surrender sovereign Ukrainian territory, including its heavily fortified defensive positions in Donbas.
“This is in addition to the constant pressure from Kushner and Witkoff for Kyiv to surrender sovereign Ukrainian territory, including its fortress belt – key defensive positions preventing a rapid advance westward,” they said.
The statement accused the envoys of repeatedly bypassing, ignoring, and undermining the US intelligence community and State Department.
“Their Trumpian transactional approach, in which they are treating a nation’s fight for survival like a real estate deal, threatens global stability,” the lawmakers said.
“They and Trump are working for Putin, not for the benefit of the people of the United States.”
The accusations came as President Volodymyr Zelensky rejected US pressure to surrender territory in Donbas during a press conference in Dublin.
“The American side very often raises the topic of Donbas, part of our Ukrainian land,” Zelensky said Wednesday.
“They think that to end this war, we have to leave our territory. It’s impossible to talk this way with us, with an independent, sovereign country.”
Meeks, Smith, and Reed warned that weakening Ukraine while easing pressure on Moscow would not produce a lasting peace but would instead reward Russian aggression.
“Congress and the American people also understand that Putin responds only to strength,” they said.
“Negotiating away all the pressure from him while undercutting Ukraine has not and will never be successful.”
The lawmakers also condemned proposals that could undermine NATO’s post-Cold War security arrangements by accommodating Russian demands for a reduced Western military presence in Eastern Europe.
“Pushing a post-war security agreement that seeks to destroy NATO’s post-Cold War mandate of a ‘Europe whole, free, and at peace,’ benefits only Russia and threatens grave consequences for us and the rest of the world,” they warned.
They argued that Congress and the American public had historically supported Ukraine and NATO because doing so was both strategically sound and morally right.
The lawmakers also criticized what they described as the administration’s focus on transactional diplomacy at the expense of America’s national security interests.
The statement came ahead of Thursday’s planned meeting between Kushner, Witkoff, and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
As Kyiv Post reported , the envoys are expected to meet Putin before traveling to Dublin for further negotiations with Zelensky.
Zelensky has expressed skepticism that Moscow will provide concrete answers to proposals discussed during Abu Dhabi talks , while insisting that Washington must pressure Russia rather than demand territorial concessions from Ukraine.
Zelensky also stressed that Kyiv needs binding security guarantees from the US, not promises from Moscow.
The Democratic lawmakers concluded their statement with a direct warning to Trump, accusing his envoys of pursuing an approach that risks rewarding Russia’s invasion.
“The Administration has claimed to be in favor of ‘peace through strength.’ The president should inform Kushner and Witkoff that surrendering in Ukraine and appeasing Putin will result in neither peace nor strength.”
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Spy Scandal Sets Off New Era of China Policy for the Democratic Party
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Spy Scandal Sets Off New Era of China Policy for the Democratic Party
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
A relationship between the high-profile CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang and a businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing has sent shockwaves through political and technology circles.
Alice Huang , who worked in Chinese finance before moving into tech with a leadership position at a Singapore data center firm, reportedly maintained a close relationship with the head of the California company whose chips power advanced artificial intelligence systems.
Reporting over the past month by the New York Times revealed that top policymakers received a memo outlining intelligence that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an operative for China’s Ministry of State Security. The intelligence indicated she had been recruited to sway Nvidia into making its top-tier microchips more accessible within China.
A widely shared 2024 photograph, uploaded to LinkedIn by software firm NetThunder, captures Jensen Huang and others holding drinks in Taipei, with Alice Huang seated behind him, seemingly watching him speak.
The precise duration of the affair and the timing of its conclusion remain unknown and Alice Huang couldn’t be reached for comment.
Very little publicly available information exists regarding Alice Huang. She worked as a Chinese finance executive before transitioning into the artificial intelligence, data center, and computer chip sectors.
In 2023, Huang became a director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a firm that characterizes itself as an "NVIDIA cloud partner." The business faced scrutiny from the U.S. last year over allegations of circumventing U.S. export restrictions and routing significant quantities of advanced Nvidia chips to users in China.
Corporate registration records show Megaspeed was originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, functioning as an overseas spin-off for a Chinese video game developer.
Filings reveal that the business rebranded as Megaspeed International in March 2023, with all shares being transferred to Huang Le Limited, an entity registered in the British Virgin Islands.
That same month, research from C4ADS, a Washington-based non-profit focused on global security, showed that Alice Huang became the controlling shareholder of Megaspeed.
However, by November 2023, Huang was no longer listed as a director at Megaspeed, and her full shareholding was transferred to Tan Yong Pong, a Singaporean businessman who is also known as James Tan.
While public documents indicate Alice Huang departed Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research published a report in May citing a company employee who stated Huang was "actually still our boss" and remained involved in daily operations.
Before her involvement with Megaspeed, Alice Huang held senior executive positions at Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to records from Chinese private equity database Simuwang and social media posts.
According to social media posts by Hexi, her roles there included deputy general manager, executive director, and member of the investment committee, among potential other responsibilities.
Hexi's founder Kang Wei, whose name appeared alongside Alice Huang on certain records, was fined 400,000 yuan ($60,000) by China's securities regulator in 2018 over financial misconduct, while Hexi itself received a fine of 17.7 million yuan ($2.7 million).
Prior to that, Alice Huang worked within HSBC’s private banking division in Hong Kong and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank.
Neither HSBC nor CITIC immediately responded to requests for comment regarding her employment history.
When questioned by lawmakers and reporters this week about Megaspeed and Alice Huang, Taiwan’s Interior Minister Liu Shyh-fang stated that authorities, including national security officials, are "actively" investigating the matter, adding that Huang would be prevented from returning to Taiwan.
Beijing has denied allegations that Alice Huang was working as a Chinese operative. The Foreign Ministry stated this week that the "Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China."
With the emergence of the latest scandal, Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a senior executive, is once again in the spotlight.
Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was originally incorporated in 2015 before changing its name to Megaspeed International in 2023. Nvidia lists Megaspeed as a partner on its website, while Megaspeed says on its website it's “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region.”
It was the overseas gaming arm of Shenzhen-based developer 7Road Holdings Ltd.
Late last year, Megaspeed denied accusations following reports that it was routing Nvidia chips to China, saying in a statement on its website that “there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities.”
Singapore’s government said in late October, after fresh reports that Alice Huang was accused of being a Chinese intelligence source, that authorities were investigating Megaspeed and that Singapore “does not condone businesses” circumventing or violating other countries’ export controls. However, it said, there were no investigations conducted in respect to Alice Huang.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Young people to be stripped of main disability benefits
articles.title_zh: Young people to be stripped of main disability benefits
articles.content_orig:
Young people will no longer be able to claim the main disability benefits under a significant welfare overhaul to be unveiled later this month.
Alan Milburn, a former health secretary, is expected to say in a long-awaited review into the youth worklessness crisis that the benefits system should be rebuilt “from scratch”.
In an interview with The Times , he said the plans – which aim to bring down the number of young people not in education, employment or training – will not be “pain-free”.
Under the proposals, young people will no longer be able to claim personal independence payments (PIPs) or the health element of universal credit.
They would instead be moved to a new “youth allowance” which would pay them the same amount of money as the standard rate of universal credit.
Meanwhile many other PIP claimants would move to a new additional-cost allowance, which would help them cover the extra costs of managing their conditions.
This allowance would not be means-tested and people who do not work would be able to claim it, but fewer people are set to be entitled to it.
The changes will apply to existing as well as new claimants, and those with the most serious conditions who are deemed unable to work would be protected.
Mr Milburn, who served under Sir Tony Blair, is expected to call for people with mild attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism and anxiety to be given immediate mental health support .
The plans, first reported by The Times, are expected to be unveiled alongside an employment support package for young people which could cost billions.
Last week, The Telegraph revealed the review will recommend spending £6bn more on getting people back into work .
Young people who do not engage with the extra support they are offered are expected to lose some of the benefits under the plans.
Mr Milburn said the plans would require “significant” extra spending and suggested they would not bring the benefits bill down in the short-term.
However Andy Burnham is under pressure to reduce welfare spending, but has refused to make “crude” cuts to the bill.
The Office for Budget Responsibility expects the UK’s welfare bill will total £333bn this year. By the end of the decade, the annual cost will have climbed to £407bn.
Plans by Sir Keir Starmer to cut £5bn from the benefits bill last year led to a rebellion by more than 80 Labour MPs, and dealt a significant blow to the former prime minister’s authority.
Mr Milburn said: “Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.
“But actually, for young people, there’s a different debate that we’ve got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.
“I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that’s the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around.
“The approach I’ve taken on this is to try to define what would give young people the best chance of building a good life, not just over a year or two, but over the course of their lifetimes.”
He said the changes amounted to a “big rewiring” of the welfare system and added: “And obviously one of the conundrums was, should this apply to only new claimants?
“I came to the conclusion that wouldn’t be right, not least because you’ve got hundreds of thousands of young people stuck in a benefit system that is trapping them in poverty, giving them no prospect of prosperity or a job.
“That conclusion makes it difficult politically because it means people are getting a current entitlement and that entitlement is going to change. But it needs to.
“You’ve got to invest upfront in order to get savings out of the back end. ‘Cost-free’ is fatuous. So we’ve got to be candid about that. It will need significant investment.
“To get a return on investment will take time … the only way of cutting the benefits bill sustainably is by getting young people into work, paying their taxes and being less reliant on benefits. Unless you are prepared to put the investment upfront it will never be possible.”
Kemi Badenoch has unveiled plans to cut £36bn from the benefits bill, while Reform UK says it has found £50bn of savings.
Last month, Mrs Badenoch outlined proposals to ban young people from signing straight on to benefits, and will require under-25s with less than six months of continuous employment to undergo intensive job coaching instead of claiming universal credit.

CoreWeave ( CRWV ) stock surged as much as 25% on Wednesday after the neocloud infrastructure provider reported better-than-expected quarterly revenue and raised its revenue outlook, fueled by booming customer demand for AI compute capacity.
The company highlighted $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months, and said it does not plan to take on more expensive debt through 2027, easing concerns about how it will fund its expansion.
"Demand for compute is growing faster than the capacity to deliver that infrastructure and that is being echoed by the expansion of the margins that we are seeing on each additional contract," CoreWeave co-founder and CEO Michael Intrator said during the company's earnings call on Tuesday after the bell.
The company reported $3.66 billion in third quarter revenue versus consensus estimates of $3.56 billion, according to Bloomberg data. CoreWeave's loss per share of $1.27 came in narrower than the $1.46 expected by Wall Street. The company also raised its full-year revenue guidance to $13 billion to $13.3 billion, up from a prior target of $12 billion to $13 billion.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
CoreWeave stock has been battered in recent weeks, dropping more than 40% over the past month amid growing concerns about AI financing. A chart that went viral in October showed CoreWeave's spiking bond yields, underscoring concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet and whether it can scale its business quickly enough to cover rising interest expenses.
Amid the sell-off, Nvidia ( NVDA ) CEO Jensen Huang tried to ease concerns about the company's debt-heavy balance sheet by stating he was "optimistic" and that its "cost of capital is actually decreasing."

articles.title_orig: Some under-25s should get less benefits, Milburn review to say
articles.title_zh: Some under-25s should get less benefits, Milburn review to say
articles.content_orig:
Some young people could see reductions to the benefits they are entitled to, under a radical overhaul of the system to be recommended by a government-commissioned review.
Alan Milburn's year-long report, which will be published on Tuesday, will recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits, the Times reported .
Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, has been tasked by the government with helping reduce the one in eight 18- to 24-year-olds in the UK who are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet".
He said on Wednesday night that his plans would not be "pain-free" and would affect both existing and new claimants.
His report is expected to recommend that under-25s are no longer able to claim the health element of universal credit or personal independence payment (Pip).
Instead, they would receive an allowance on the same basic rate as universal credit.
Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to their conditions.
But many claimants would receive less under the plans, which the government is set to take forward into legislation in the new year.
Milburn, a Labour MP from 1992 to 2010, is also expected to recommend an investment of billions into more employment support for young people, including work placements, job subsidies and one-to-one personal advisers.
Those with more severe disabilities and unable to work would get a new benefit paid at a higher rate.
Speaking to the Times about his report, Milburn said: "Candidly, it could mean that some people will get less financial support at the beginning of their benefit claim than under the current system.
"But actually, for young people, there's a different debate that we've got to resolve, which is whether the priority is their longer-term life chances or just their immediate shorter-term finances.
"I think what the current system does [is] it prioritises the latter over the former. I believe that's the wrong choice and it needs to be the other way around."
Just under one million young people in the UK are Neets , data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from April to June suggests. This was a rise of 3% on the same period last year.
Milburn's recommendations are likely to be backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham but could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who opposed welfare reform under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.
The reforms would represent a radical overhaul of Britain's welfare system, at a time when there is heavy political pressure for the UK to find the money to spend more on defence.
If Milburn's recommendations were approved, it could take almost a decade for the British state to see monetary savings.
The new system "will need significant investment" and would involve "rebuilding the system from scratch," Milburn added.
He said that currently "you've got hundreds of thousands of young people stuck in a benefit system that is trapping them in poverty, giving them no prospect of prosperity or a job".
His new proposed system would involve an element of carrot and stick, where young people could lose some of their benefits if they did not engage with the extra work support options.
"A deal isn't a deal unless there are potential consequences," Milburn said. "Entitlements and responsibilities are two sides of the same coin."
A government spokesperson said: "We will always ensure there is a safety net for the most vulnerable and those who are unable to work.
"But the prime minister has been clear that we need a wholesale change in the way we support young people to grow up in this country, where we invest in their success rather than paying for failure."

articles.title_orig: Iran escalates in Hormuz, claims strike on Omani island it says 'enemy' uses for US military ops
articles.title_zh: Iran escalates in Hormuz, claims strike on Omani island it says 'enemy' uses for US military ops
articles.content_orig:
The IRGC reported a strike against ‘enemy navigation aid systems,’ radar and communications equipment located on Didamar Island in Hormuz (Credit: Reuters).
Iran claims it struck a small Omani island in the Strait of Hormuz , targeting oil tanker navigation infrastructure as CENTCOM maintains its blockade of Iranian ports and protects commercial shipping from Iranian attacks along the southern route.
Three sources also confirmed to Reuters Wednesday that navigation systems and communications equipment on Didamar Island, also known as Little Quoin Island, had been attacked, raising concerns about the vulnerability of maritime infrastructure used to maintain oil shipments through the Gulf.
Iran's semiofficial Fars News Agency reported that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy targeted the island, alleging the systems were being used to help vessels transit the strait without Tehran's authorization.
WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON IRAN-OMAN HORMUZ PLAN TEHRAN SAYS WOULD BAN US WARSHIPS
A satellite image shows Didamar Island, Oman (Google/Airbus/Handout via Reuters)
Iranian state television also claimed that personnel and equipment on the island "were helping the flow of oil smuggling by the enemy," with the IRGC maintaining it had carried out the strikes, Reuters reported.
Video published by Reuters showed smoke rising near the rocky outcrop.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said it identified the attack as occurring Nov. 8, before Iranian state media claimed responsibility on Nov. 10.
ISW also questioned the extent of the reported damage, noting that commercial vessels continued using the southern route after the attack.
"The extent of the damage to these systems and the systems struck remains unclear at the time of this writing," ISW said in its assessment.
Satellite imagery from the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 program, cited by Reuters and dated Nov. 8, also showed apparent scorch marks near radar and radio equipment on the island.
TRADE VESSEL STRUCK BY PROJECTILE IN STRAIT OF HORMUZ AMID US-IRAN TALKS
A ship passes through the Strait of Hormuz during a two-week temporary ceasefire between the United States and Iran April 8, 2026. (Shady Alassar/Anadolu/Getty Images)
The strike comes as U.S. forces carry out missions to escort ships through the Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.
The U.S. Navy imposed its blockade of Iranian ports in April after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in February amid escalating tensions. The U.S. lifted the blockade in June following a temporary ceasefire agreement, but then reinstated it in July.
Commercial and allied shipping through the waterway is advised to use a southern route through Omani territorial waters, located outside of Tehran’s direct military control and overseen by CENTCOM.
The latest incident on Didamar Island comes as Gulf oil exporters work to restore shipments disrupted by the conflict.
TRUMP MEETS KEY IRAN WAR MEDIATOR AS UAE REVEALS MAJOR OIL EXPORT SURGE DESPITE CONFLICT
An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps speedboat sails in the Persian Gulf during an IRGC marine parade marking Persian Gulf National Day near the Bushehr nuclear power plant in Bushehr, Iran, April 29, 2024. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
According to Reuters, regional oil exports recovered to more than 80% of prewar levels in September and October, aided by CENTCOM and increased Saudi exports through the Red Sea.
Shipping companies have also relied on offshore tanker-to-tanker transfers near Oman and the United Arab Emirates to maintain flows.
Didamar, meanwhile, belongs to Oman, making the reported attack particularly sensitive as Tehran seeks to disrupt maritime operations in the region. It is a small, uninhabited rocky island roughly 10 nautical miles north of the tip of Oman's Musandam Peninsula, near one of the principal commercial shipping routes through the strait.
The island has long served as a navigational landmark for vessels traveling along the waterway, including through a lighthouse established in 1914.
Its maritime infrastructure reportedly includes a radar system mounted on a roughly 25-meter tower and radio communications equipment used to assist vessels navigating the narrow passage.
The island has also been associated with the Hormuz Control Centre, which coordinates maritime traffic in the area.
OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES
A satellite image shows the Strait of Hormuz, a key maritime passage connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, vital for global energy supply. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)
Arabian Maritime and Navigation Aids Services (AMMAS) has been identified as a provider of navigational support infrastructure in the region, including maritime lights, buoys and other equipment.
The reported Didamar attack also follows U.S. military operations against Iranian targets elsewhere in the waterway.
U.S. forces struck targets on Iran's Qeshm Island Nov. 2, and officials described the strikes as "defensive" actions targeting Iranian surface-to-air missile threats.
Qeshm Island, located near the Strait of Hormuz, is home to Iranian naval facilities and military infrastructure associated with the Revolutionary Guard.
President Donald Trump also acknowledged Nov. 6 that American forces continue to conduct limited strikes against Iranian targets.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Asked by a reporter about the strikes near Qeshm Island, Trump said, "I don't want to talk about it. We do minor strikes. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five."
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title_orig: Lutnick stalled Trump crackdown on diversion of Nvidia chips to China, Axios reports
articles.title_zh: Lutnick stalled Trump crackdown on diversion of Nvidia chips to China, Axios reports
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Cloud computing firm Megaspeed has come under fresh scrutiny as the US looks into Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy .
Nvidia has seen hundreds of billions of dollars wiped from its value in recent days after the US chipmaker said it would investigate Huang’s admitted relationship with the former Megaspeed director Alice Huang .
China says allegations about Chinese spies are “entirely groundless” and “intended to smear and malign China”. But US intelligence officials nevertheless believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was funneling information to Beijing .
For years, Washington has tried to keep China from gaining the know-how to rival the United States in cutting-edge AI, which Nvidia’s chips support.
Now attention turns to Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Beijing ‌gain access ⁠to advanced AI chips whose export to China is restricted.
Megaspeed was incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International before changing its name to Megaspeed International in March 2023, when it was bought by a British Virgin Islands company called Huang Le Ltd.
Alice Huang ended her eight month tenure as managing director months later, in October 2023, but is reported to still be involved in the company. In November 2023, the firm was sold again to a Singaporean entity called Swiftdata, which says its main job is providing hosting services by non-data centres.
Megaspeed's assets increased sharply to $3 billion in 2024 from $33 million in 2023, its business filings showed.
The company soon became one of Nvidia’s biggest Asian customers and grew rapidly as a link between the US chipmaker and the Chinese tech group Alibaba. Two Singapore citizens are listed as officers of both Megaspeed and Swiftdata.
Singapore has come under mounting pressure from the US to clamp down on companies suspected of transferring advanced AI chips to Chinese firms. But the city-state does not necessarily exclude such transfers.
Singaporean police are now conducting their own investigation into Megaspeed, in step with US authorities. US intelligence officials have already concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to the New York Times .
US intelligence officials have reportedly been alert to Alice Huang’s position for some time. According to the New York Times , US president Donald Trump was briefed on intelligence findings around a year ago but chose to do nothing with them.
It was late last year that US authorities began investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it was helping to divert Nvidia chips to China.
Singapore police said they would investigate the firm over “suspected breaches of our domestic laws” after a US senator asked the commerce department to look into related concerns.
According to the NYT, officials suspected it was Alice Huang who was feeding information directly to Beijing on how to gain access to the advanced AI chips.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and told the newspaper that it was “committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations” and would welcome a “formal, evidence-based investigation”.
It said in a statement last year that “there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities”.
And Nvidia said Megaspeed was just like any other regional customer, and that such customers only “receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security”.
For all the concerns above, the affair between Alice Huang and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has rocked the tech and political worlds. It remains unclear how long the affair lasted, and when exactly the relationship might have ended.
Alice Huang was a Chinese finance executive before becoming involved in artificial intelligence, data centers and computer chips. She became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder in March 2023, according to research by the C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on global security.
But by November 2023, she was no longer listed as a director, and all her shares were transferred to a Singaporean businessman, Tan Yong Pong, who also is known as James Tan.
While public records suggest Alice Huang left Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research issued a report in May this year that cited a Megaspeed employee saying Huang was “actually still our boss” and was still involved in the company’s daily operations.
Before Megaspeed, Alice Huang previously held senior positions at the Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database.
Before that, she worked at HSBC’s Hong Kong private banking arm and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank.
